findings.title: The learner receives incompatible runtime contracts for the same gate.
findings.evidence: Outcome requires Python 3.12+, multiple paragraphs say 3.10+ is acceptable, while Ruff target-version is py312.
findings.impact: A learner on 3.10 cannot determine whether to continue, upgrade, or alter Ruff; subsequent reproducibility evidence no longer has one target runtime.
findings.fix: Choose one supported floor and state it everywhere. Current roadmap and config point to 3.12+.
findings.location: learning outcomes + interpreter paragraphs + stack verification + Ruff config
findings.prior_knowledge: none

findings.title: The example uses future syntax to teach a concept that can be demonstrated with one print statement, and the callout falsely makes def + __name__ guard sound necessary for scripts.
findings.evidence: The first script introduces import, def, indentation, variables, method calls, indexing, f-strings and if __name__ before those concepts are taught; the callout says a .py uses def + if __name__.
findings.impact: The learner memorizes a template without being able to explain or predict its parts and can incorrectly believe every script requires main() and an __name__ guard.
findings.fix: Replace the first script with a single print statement; defer main/import/f-string/__name__ until their real teaching sections.
findings.prior_knowledge: ZERO_TECH plus interpreter/REPL from immediately preceding paragraphs
findings.cross_section: S02 f-strings; S03 conditionals; S05 functions; later modules/imports

findings.title: A transcript and an executable command block are represented as the same thing.
findings.evidence: The prose calls the block 'copy-paste real'; it starts an interactive python3 REPL but the following REPL commands are shell-style commented transcript lines, so pasting the full block cannot execute the demonstrated interaction and exit as claimed.
findings.impact: The learner pastes the block, enters the REPL, comments out the supposed expressions/quit command, and gets stuck or sends later shell commands to Python.
findings.fix: Label it as a transcript or split shell commands and REPL keystrokes into separate clearly typed blocks.
findings.location: theory block 'El intérprete en la terminal' code
findings.prior_knowledge: basic terminal actions just introduced

findings.title: The learner must understand several later Python constructs to understand the example used for a much simpler process contract.
findings.evidence: S01 teaches sys.argv as a list, indexing, len, slicing, stderr, a function, conditional and type annotation to demonstrate exit codes.
findings.impact: The learner can only copy check_arg.py and cannot explain why len==2, what [1:] means, or why the branch exits 1.
findings.fix: Remove argv/slicing from S01 theory and demonstrate exit 0/1 with prepared one-liners; teach CLI arguments in the later CLI section.
findings.location: theory block 'Terminal, rutas y códigos de salida' argv paragraph + check_arg.py
findings.prior_knowledge: ZERO_TECH plus exit-code concept

findings.title: The error-suppression example undermines the core mental model rather than extending it safely.
findings.evidence: The lesson emphasizes exit status as evidence, then introduces 2>/dev/null || true as a starter pattern without saying that || true can turn a failure into overall success and erase the signal just taught.
findings.impact: The learner can adopt 'append || true when a command is noisy/fails' and cause a script or CI step to report success after a real failure.
findings.fix: Remove this pattern from core S01. If retained in optional troubleshooting, explicitly explain that it masks failure and is valid only when failure is intentionally non-fatal.
findings.location: 'Leer una línea de terminal' final paragraph
findings.prior_knowledge: exit-code contract from immediately preceding theory

findings.title: A privacy-sensitive first-day workflow asks the learner to persist a real email globally without informed choice.
findings.evidence: The lesson instructs git config --global user.email 'tu@correo.com' immediately before publishing to GitHub, but gives no warning that commit email metadata can expose a personal address or that GitHub provides a noreply address.
findings.impact: A learner follows the command literally, pushes a public repository and exposes a personal email in commit metadata.
findings.fix: Before the command, explain commit-email visibility and offer the GitHub noreply address; advise --local when personal/work identities differ.
findings.location: Git identity paragraph + git config code
findings.prior_knowledge: ZERO_TECH and the lesson's own privacy/secret model

findings.title: The time promise cannot be satisfied at the upper end and the phrase 'resto' has no coherent remainder in a 10 h section.
findings.evidence: Tagline allocates 3–4 h to core plus 6–8 h to GitHub/Ruff plus remaining time for CP-N1-A, while theory states about 10 h total.
findings.impact: The learner cannot tell what is core, optional, or expected within the advertised section duration and may interpret unfinished material as personal failure.
findings.fix: Make the tagline express a 10 h allocation whose parts sum to the total, and define CP-N1-A when first named.
findings.prior_knowledge: none

findings.title: NASA identifies a failed use/translation of required metric units plus verification, communication and systems-engineering contributing causes; the prose over-absolves the failure mechanism.
findings.evidence: The Mars Climate Orbiter paragraph says nobody made a calculation error and reduces the mishap to two teams assuming different units.
findings.impact: The learner forms an oversimplified causal model in the very example used to justify explicit contracts and verification.
findings.fix: Keep the incident but state the metric/English-unit interface failure and that project controls did not detect it.
findings.prior_knowledge: none

findings.title: Internal curriculum identifiers are used as though they carry meaning for a first-day learner.
findings.evidence: CP-N1-A and CASO-LIM-001 appear before a learner-facing explanation of what those labels represent.
findings.impact: The learner must infer whether CP-N1-A/CASO-LIM-001 are tools, files, assignments or projects and may search outside the lesson.
findings.fix: At first occurrence add a microdefinition such as 'el caso de práctica de esta sección' and 'el proyecto acumulativo de Nivel 1'.
findings.prior_knowledge: none

findings.title: Remote execution is not a defining property of a script.
findings.evidence: Caption defines a script as a file that runs whole 'en una máquina que no es la tuya', while the prose tells the learner to run python hello.py locally.
findings.impact: The learner may classify local .py execution as something other than a script or associate scripts primarily with servers/pipelines.
findings.fix: Define the contrast as interactive one-expression-at-a-time execution versus saved-file execution; remove the remote-machine property.
findings.prior_knowledge: interpreter and REPL introduced locally

findings.title: The learner receives an inaccurate forward map of when this syntax becomes learnable.
findings.evidence: Type annotation paragraph says annotations return when S02–S03 deepen types, while roadmap places gradual type hints from S05; S03 is decisions/validation, not type-hint instruction.
findings.impact: The learner may interpret absence of type-hint teaching in S03 as missing content or believe type annotations are part of basic value types.
findings.fix: Either remove the forward section numbers or point to the actual section where annotations are deliberately taught.
findings.prior_knowledge: none

findings.title: Terminal and shell change from distinct conceptual levels into synonyms.
findings.evidence: Opening defines terminal as the text window; later prose calls bash, zsh and PowerShell 'la terminal'.
findings.impact: A Windows learner cannot understand why the same terminal application can host PowerShell or another shell with different syntax.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: terminal is the application/window; shell is the command interpreter inside it, e.g. PowerShell, bash or zsh.
findings.location: opening definitions + 'Terminal, rutas y códigos de salida'
findings.prior_knowledge: none

findings.title: Too many independent shell operators and platform branches must be held in working memory before they are needed for the section's core reproducibility model.
findings.evidence: Before the learner reaches venv, one block adds >, >>, |, head, grep, &&, ||, mkdir, rm -rf, which/where and stderr redirection.
findings.impact: When a later venv/pip command fails, the learner has to distinguish environment failure from a large new shell syntax vocabulary and may debug the wrong layer.
findings.fix: Keep only commands required immediately; move pipes/filters/error redirection/destructive cleanup to optional reference or introduce each immediately before first essential use.
findings.location: 'Leer una línea de terminal: los conectores del día 1'
findings.prior_knowledge: ordinary files/folders only

findings.title: The isolation model is stronger than the portability model actually guaranteed by venv.
findings.evidence: The environment is repeatedly described as a self-contained folder with 'its own Python'; Python documentation says venvs are disposable and not considered movable/copyable.
findings.impact: The learner can conclude that copying .venv to another machine is a valid reproducibility strategy because the folder supposedly contains a self-contained Python.
findings.fix: Define it as an isolated directory with a Python associated with that environment and its site-packages, then explicitly say it is recreated rather than copied.
findings.location: jobRelevance + opening environment definition + venv paragraph
findings.prior_knowledge: none

findings.title: A platform-specific failure mode interrupts the first exposure before the learner has stabilized the base concept.
findings.evidence: Debian/Ubuntu ensurepip/package-manager recovery is embedded in the first core definition of venv.
findings.impact: A learner on macOS/Windows must process apt, ensurepip and distro packaging despite none being relevant; a Linux learner sees recovery syntax before understanding what successful creation should mean.
findings.fix: Move distro-specific repair into a troubleshooting callout after the successful model and verification.
findings.prior_knowledge: none

findings.title: The learner is told what suffix the output should have without understanding why that value proves the active environment.
findings.evidence: sys.prefix is used as proof that the venv is active but the lesson does not define what sys.prefix represents.
findings.impact: The learner pattern-matches '.venv' rather than understanding the diagnostic and cannot adapt it when paths differ.
findings.fix: Add a microdefinition: sys.prefix is the directory Python reports as the active environment prefix.
findings.prior_knowledge: none

findings.title: The example advertises the reconstruction action central to reproducibility but only demonstrates install/freeze/import in the same environment.
findings.evidence: The code block is titled 'install, freeze, install -r' but never executes python -m pip install -r requirements.txt.
findings.impact: The learner may think they have seen/tested the clean reconstruction step when the code never performs it.
findings.fix: Either rename the block to its actual scope or add an explicit clean-environment install -r demonstration without pretending same-venv reinstall proves portability.
findings.prior_knowledge: venv/pip just taught

findings.title: The recovery contract is incomplete for the exact novice state most likely to contain newly created untracked files.
findings.evidence: The prose says git stash stores temporary changes and leaves the tree clean without stating that untracked files are not included by default; Git documents -u/--include-untracked for that behavior.
findings.impact: The learner stashes before switching context, assumes a clean tree, and is surprised that new untracked files remain; they may then misdiagnose Git or accidentally leave sensitive files exposed.
findings.fix: Say stash handles tracked modifications by default; use git stash -u only when deliberately including untracked files, and verify with git status.
findings.prior_knowledge: Git status/add/commit from previous block

findings.title: A key security artifact is demonstrated with syntax a Windows learner cannot execute, while another unexplained delivery concept is used to justify Ruff.
findings.evidence: CI is used without a microdefinition; the core .gitignore/.env.example creation block uses Bash heredoc syntax even though S01 promises Windows PowerShell support.
findings.impact: The Windows learner receives a syntax error when creating .gitignore and cannot know whether Git, the file content or the shell is wrong; the CI comparison adds an unexplained dependency.
findings.fix: Define CI in one clause and create these tiny files through VS Code with content blocks, then verify with git check-ignore; avoid heredoc as the canonical cross-platform path.
findings.prior_knowledge: CI/CD and shell heredocs explicitly absent from ZERO_TECH baseline

findings.title: Does the deployed hydrated S01 page exactly match the canonical source reviewed here?
What deterministic convention guarantees that 'DNI ficticios' cannot accidentally reuse a real Peruvian identifier when synthetic CSV data are created?
findings.justification: Potential privacy/data-quality issue; not promoted to a confirmed finding without the actual dataset generation contract.

findings.title: Premature knowledge: basic runtime/reproducibility concepts are taught through Python syntax reserved for later sections.
Cross-platform and evidence inconsistency: some canonical examples are labelled executable/cross-platform but are transcripts or Bash-only.
Safety/model gaps: commit-email privacy, venv portability and stash behavior are materially underexplained or overgeneralized.

A syntax scaffold belonging to S05 is used as the container for S02's first worked examples, so the learner must parse a function before focusing on the value/type concept the example claims to teach.
findings.evidence: Every main theory example is wrapped in def s02_th_*() or defines safe_int(...); several also carry annotations such as campo: str and valor: str. The V3 roadmap schedules function definition/call/return/parameters and gradual type hints in S05.
findings.impact: The learner copies def/indentation/call syntax as ritual, cannot explain why the body is indented or why s02_th_1() runs, and may infer that small Python examples require a function wrapper.
findings.fix: Make S02 theory examples top-level statements. Refactor into functions only when S05 teaches functions; do not add a mini S05 to S02.
findings.location: all non-optional theory code blocks and optional contract code
findings.prior_knowledge: S01 USABLE concepts only; function syntax was MENTION_ONLY in S01 and receives no credit.

findings.title: Calling control flow 'support syntax' does not make it cognitively inert: the learner must understand branch selection and iteration to predict the examples.
findings.evidence: The lesson announces that if and for will appear as support syntax. safe_int depends on if; T2-A uses if/else; the figure explains truthiness; for iterates test values. V3 assigns truthiness/if/elif/else to S03 and for to S04.
findings.impact: The learner can recite what int() does but cannot explain why safe_int returns one tuple instead of another or why the for block executes multiple conversions.
findings.fix: Remove if/else/for/truthiness from core S02 theory examples. Demonstrate conversions with separate concrete inputs and show errors directly; defer branching/iteration to S03/S04.
findings.location: opening paragraph 6; T1-B; T2-A code; T2-B truthiness figure; parser code
findings.prior_knowledge: No control-flow or iteration mastery.

findings.title: The lesson requires exception handling to make its main parser outcome work but never teaches what an exception is, where control jumps, or why only a specific exception should be caught.
findings.evidence: try/except, ValueError capture, InvalidOperation capture, 'no tragar excepciones' and except: pass are central to the parser explanation. V3 places exceptions and recovery boundaries in S09.
findings.impact: The learner treats try/except as magic punctuation and cannot predict whether the return after try runs, whether except runs, or what happens for an unexpected error.
findings.fix: Either teach a deliberately bounded micro-model of one recoverable ValueError before the first try/except, or defer robust recovery until S09 and keep S02 to successful conversion plus observable failing examples. Do not silently rely on S09 knowledge.
findings.location: T1-B and T4-B safe_int; T3-B InvalidOperation prose
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner has seen error names but has not learned an exception mental model or try/except execution semantics.
findings.cross_section: S09; roadmap gate also expects invalid-number handling and therefore needs reconciliation

findings.title: A minimal mutable-container preview for aliasing is defensible under the S02 roadmap, but the lesson expands that preview into tuple protocols, slicing, unpacking and typed lists required to follow the parser.
findings.evidence: The parser contract returns three-element tuples, for iterates a list, T2-B uses list literals/append/copy/a[:], T3-A uses a,b,c = 10,3,2, and T4-B names list[str]. V3 puts lists/tuples/slicing/unpacking in S06, while S02 only permits identity/mutability/copies 'al nivel necesario'.
findings.impact: The learner must infer bracket/tuple/unpacking semantics and the shape of (ok, value, message) before knowing what a tuple is, obscuring conversion and validation.
findings.fix: Keep one explicitly introduced list solely for aliasing/mutability, with a one-sentence definition. Remove tuple-return protocols, slicing, unpacking and list[str] from S02 core; revisit them in S06.
findings.location: T1-B tuple contract; T2-B list/copy/slice; T3-A tuple unpacking; T4-B errors:list[str]
findings.prior_knowledge: No collection syntax from S01.

findings.title: The lesson turns a mutation guarantee into an identity guarantee.
findings.evidence: The prose states that .strip() or concatenation returns another string. Immutability guarantees that the original string is not mutated, not that a distinct object identity must be produced; implementations may reuse the original object when the result is unchanged.
findings.impact: The learner can predict s is s.strip() must always be False and use identity to reason about string transformations, which is not a valid contract.
findings.fix: Replace 'devuelve otro string' with 'produce un resultado str sin modificar el original; no bases la lógica en si Python reutiliza o no el mismo objeto'.
findings.prior_knowledge: Identity vs equality is the exact topic being taught.

findings.title: A rule presented as Python-wide changes for the numeric type immediately introduced in T3-B.
findings.evidence: T3-A states / returns float and // rounds toward -infinity without restricting operand types. In the same section Decimal division returns Decimal, and Decimal // truncates toward zero (e.g. Decimal(-7)//Decimal(4) == Decimal(-1), while -7//4 == -2).
findings.impact: The learner applies the int rule to Decimal and predicts the wrong type or wrong negative quotient.
findings.fix: Scope the rule explicitly: 'con int, / produce float y // hace floor; otros tipos pueden definir estos operadores de otra manera'. In T3-B state Decimal's difference only if // or % will actually be used.
findings.location: T3-A operator definitions vs T3-B Decimal
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic types plus Decimal introduced next.

findings.title: Approximation error is mislabeled as non-reproducibility, changing the meaning of a core S01 term, and the figure's universal rounding rule conflicts with the paragraph's boundary-based rule.
findings.evidence: The caption says 'con float ni siquiera es reproducible' and 'Redondear una sola vez, al final', while the prose later says quantize at each monetary step that must be shown or persisted. Python documents float's issue as binary representation/round-off, and even provides exact hexadecimal representations useful for reliable portability.
findings.impact: The learner can believe repeated float operations are random/non-repeatable and cannot tell whether to round once globally or at each defined business boundary.
findings.fix: Caption: 'Float representa muchos decimales como aproximaciones binarias. Define una política de redondeo y aplícala en los límites de negocio que correspondan; no redondees repetidamente sin una regla'.
findings.prior_knowledge: S01 taught reproducibility as the ability to reproduce an environment/result contract.

findings.title: The worked example does not demonstrate the behavior the paragraph explicitly promises.
findings.evidence: The prose instructs importing Decimal, ROUND_HALF_EVEN and InvalidOperation 'las tres' because InvalidOperation will be captured 'en el mismo bloque'. The code imports only Decimal and ROUND_HALF_EVEN and contains no invalid input or exception handler.
findings.impact: The learner cannot locate where InvalidOperation is caught and may infer that quantize itself somehow handles invalid input.
findings.fix: Either remove the promise of capture from this T3-B block and defer invalid-input handling, or add a separately explained minimal invalid Decimal example once the exception-sequencing decision is resolved. Do not claim code that is absent.
findings.prior_knowledge: Whatever minimal Decimal/import model S02 supplies.

findings.title: Individual operations are often described, but the repeated x.algo(...) shape itself remains unexplained.
findings.evidence: The learner meets type(x).__name__, valor.strip(), a.copy(), b.append(), Decimal(...).quantize() and repr-like attributes without a first-use explanation of the dot form.
findings.impact: The learner cannot distinguish a function call such as int(x) from an operation attached to a value such as x.strip(), so future syntax becomes pattern copying rather than a predictable model.
findings.fix: Before first dot call add a microdefinition: 'x.metodo() pide al valor x ejecutar una operación propia; no necesitas estudiar objetos todavía'. Avoid __name__ if the attribute itself adds no learning value.
findings.prior_knowledge: No object/method mental model.

findings.title: The critical money type appears through an unexplained module/import statement.
findings.evidence: The prose says 'Importa: from decimal import ...' and code relies on from decimal import Decimal, while V3 teaches modules/imports in S10 and S01's import usage was not credited as learned.
findings.impact: The learner can copy Decimal but cannot explain why the name is unavailable without the import or what 'decimal' and 'Decimal' each refer to.
findings.fix: Add one microdefinition: 'decimal es un módulo de la biblioteca estándar; from decimal import Decimal hace disponible el nombre Decimal en este archivo'. Defer module mechanics to S10.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner knows the standard-library distinction from S01 but not import semantics.

findings.title: The optional learner-facing reference behaves like a curriculum/harness contract rather than an explanatory example and imports future syntax for no instructional gain.
findings.evidence: s02_map_contract.py exposes internal-looking flags such as if_for_as_support_syntax, real_pii_ok, gates and focus inside a function returning a dict/list before any of those structures are taught.
findings.impact: A novice may assume these identifiers are required course API or try to understand dict/list/function syntax that is unrelated to S02's mental model.
findings.fix: Keep the optional contract as prose/table. Remove the executable internal contract until the structures it uses have been taught.
findings.location: optional theory block 'Contrato de la sección' code
findings.prior_knowledge: ZERO_TECH plus S01 USABLE.

findings.title: A central artifact is named with English/internal labels before the learner is told that it is simply the program/script that turns captured text into interpreted fields while preserving originals.
findings.evidence: 'parser de intake', 'intake', CASO-LIM-002 and CP-N1-A are used before a learner-facing definition; parser is only concretely explained in T4-B. CP-N1-A remained unresolved at S01 entry state.
findings.impact: The learner can mistake parser/intake/CP identifiers for tools, libraries or files and must infer what is being built.
findings.fix: At first use write 'captura inicial (intake)' and 'parser, el código que transforma el texto capturado en campos interpretados'; expand CP-N1-A/CASO-LIM-002 once in learner language.
findings.prior_knowledge: No business-process or curriculum-ID vocabulary beyond ordinary form use.

findings.title: Too many interacting constructs are required before the novice can stabilize the simpler conversion model 'text -> cleaned text -> attempted int'.
findings.evidence: Within one subtopic the learner encounters type, isinstance, bool-as-int edge behavior, and/not, constructors, strip, ValueError, eval, tuples, lists, try/except, function definition, annotations, if, return and for.
findings.impact: Working memory is spent decoding syntax, so the learner can execute safe_int without retaining why conversion succeeds or fails.
findings.fix: Use worked examples that fade gradually: first int('19'), then a failing int('abc') and its error, then only the minimum recovery pattern justified by the resolved roadmap decision.
findings.prior_knowledge: Only literals/types from T1-A.

findings.title: A third assignment-like token increases interference without being needed by any S02 outcome.
findings.evidence: The walrus operator := is introduced while the novice is still separating = from ==.
findings.impact: The learner leaves the paragraph with three visually similar operators and no practical reason to use one of them.
findings.fix: Delete the walrus discussion from S02. Introduce it only when a later example genuinely benefits from assignment expressions.
findings.prior_knowledge: Assignment and equality are being learned now.

findings.title: Typography is presented close enough to semantics that a novice can infer uppercase creates an immutable binding.
findings.evidence: The paragraph says UPPER_CASE para constantes but never states that Python does not enforce constancy; PEP 8 describes uppercase as a naming convention.
findings.impact: The learner can believe IGV_TASA cannot be reassigned because of its spelling and later misdiagnose reassignment bugs.
findings.fix: Add: 'Es una convención de lectura; Python sí permite reasignar ese nombre'.
findings.prior_knowledge: No concept of language-enforced constants.

findings.title: 'Independizar' sounds total while 'superficial' is an unexplained qualifier.
findings.evidence: The prose says 'Para independizar: a.copy() o a[:] (copia superficial)' without explaining what superficial limits. Python's copy documentation states that a shallow copy creates a new outer compound object but inserts references to the same contained objects.
findings.impact: The learner can later mutate a nested list through one shallow copy and conclude copy() is broken because the nested element also changed in the other.
findings.fix: Add one boundary sentence: 'La lista exterior es nueva; si contiene objetos mutables dentro, esos objetos todavía pueden compartirse. Verás copias anidadas en S06'.
findings.prior_knowledge: No nested collections yet.

findings.title: A language-library default is too easily read as a universal business/legal policy.
findings.evidence: ROUND_HALF_EVEN is described as the usual/default 'banking' rounding in a business context without distinguishing Python's default Decimal context from an organization's accounting/tax rule. Decimal exposes multiple rounding modes and quantize can take an explicit one.
findings.impact: The learner may hard-code HALF_EVEN for a workflow whose documented accounting, tax or contractual rule requires another mode/boundary.
findings.fix: Say 'Python Decimal's default context uses ROUND_HALF_EVEN, but the business rule must specify the required mode; here we choose HALF_EVEN only as the course convention'.
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic rounding and Decimal motivation.

findings.title: A useful input() rule is generalized into a system-boundary rule that will be false in later API/JSON/data lessons.
findings.evidence: The paragraph says that in a terminal, web notebook or mobile application the boundary is essentially 'outside = text; inside = meaningful values'. input() does return str, but other application/API boundaries can deliver already-typed booleans/numbers/objects.
findings.impact: The learner can later assume every external numeric/boolean value must first exist as str and misread typed JSON/API values.
findings.fix: Limit the claim: 'Con input() y muchos campos de formulario, la entrada llega como texto; otras interfaces pueden entregar tipos distintos'.
findings.prior_knowledge: Only S02 I/O model.

findings.title: These terms are not purely decorative: they explain why code is structured a certain way or what counts as evidence.
findings.evidence: namespace, schema, pruebas unitarias, CI, asserts and pytest are used as reasons or gates before receiving learner-facing microdefinitions; S01 did not establish CI/testing and V3 places schema in S08 while systematic pytest is much later.
findings.impact: The learner must search outside PyArcana to understand why simulated input is 'testeable', what a unit test is, or what 'demos de CI' means.
findings.fix: Replace unnecessary infrastructure jargon with ordinary language now ('comprobación automática') and add one-sentence definitions only where the concept is essential. Defer schema/CI/pytest mechanics to their real sections.
findings.prior_knowledge: No namespace/schema/testing/CI concepts.

findings.title: The justification explains away syntax that actually does require a new rule.
findings.evidence: The lesson says calling print(*valores, sep=...) is merely using a function that accepts several arguments. The leading * is itself iterable argument unpacking, a distinct syntax V3 places with unpacking in S06. T4-A also presents print(*args, sep=..., end=...) before function parameter/keyword-argument models.
findings.impact: The learner may believe * has no meaning at call sites or confuse print(a,b) with print(*valores).
findings.fix: Teach print with concrete arguments only: print('a','b',sep=' | '). Do not show *valores/*args in S02; defer call-site unpacking to S06 and function-parameter semantics to S05.
findings.location: optional contract paragraph about *args and T4-A print signature
findings.prior_knowledge: No unpacking or function-parameter model.

findings.title: 'Basura' suggests random/corrupt data instead of a deterministic approximation and reinforces F15's incorrect reproducibility framing.
findings.evidence: The callout says Decimal(0.1) 'hereda la basura del float'. Python documents that Decimal(float) converts the binary float value exactly to its decimal equivalent; the issue is that the float already represents an approximation of the intended decimal 0.1.
findings.impact: The learner cannot distinguish deterministic representation error from corrupted or unstable data.
findings.fix: Replace 'basura' with 'la aproximación binaria ya contenida en ese float'.
findings.prior_knowledge: float-vs-Decimal representation model from the same block.

findings.title: Prerequisite avalanche: S02's examples import control flow, functions, collections, exceptions and modules from S03-S10.
Technical model drift: operator semantics, string identity, float reproducibility and rounding policy are stated too broadly or inconsistently.
Internal/tooling vocabulary leaks into learner-facing theory before it earns explanatory value: parser/intake IDs, namespace/schema, CI/testing and optional contract flags.

One of S03's promised T2 skills, guard clauses, inherently depends on function/return semantics that the roadmap withholds until S05, and the lesson does not teach that prerequisite before relying on it.
findings.evidence: S03 defines a guard clause as an if at the start of a function that returns immediately and almost every nontrivial example defines a function, often with return and type annotations. V3 schedules function definition/call/return/parameters/type hints in S05.
findings.impact: The learner can predict a comparison but cannot explain why return ends the route, why code below it is skipped, or why the function call produces the shown status; guard clauses become a copied shape rather than a control-flow model.
findings.fix: In S03 teach ordering/exclusivity/dead branches without early return, using top-level status assignments or direct prints. Move guard clauses/early return to S05 when functions and return are taught, or explicitly revise the roadmap if guard clauses must remain in S03.
findings.location: opening definition of guard clause; T2-A; T2-B; T3-A; T3-B; T4-A; T4-B code
findings.prior_knowledge: S01-S02 USABLE ledger only; function syntax from S01/S02 remains MENTION_ONLY.

findings.title: Iteration is used as the presentation mechanism for the very evidence the novice is supposed to inspect, so it is not incidental syntax.
findings.evidence: Worked examples repeatedly use for loops to enumerate cases and outputs before V3 teaches for/range/iteration in S04.
findings.impact: The learner cannot predict why several rows print or how variables such as s, e, c, ex, val and code change between outputs, making the decision logic harder to isolate.
findings.fix: For S03 theory, write explicit calls/prints for each case or show a static decision/example table. Introduce loops only in S04.
findings.location: T1-B, T2-A, T2-B, T3-A, T3-B, T4-A, T4-B code examples
findings.prior_knowledge: No iteration mastery.

findings.title: Structured result containers become essential to understanding status/code/message and branch tests even though the section explicitly promises not to teach collections yet.
findings.evidence: The opening callout says collections arrive later, but learner-facing theory uses set literals, dict return values, lists of tuples, nested list/dict examples, indexing such as r["code"] and ex["value"], and a dict-of-examples representation before S06 teaches collections and unpacking.
findings.impact: A novice can follow accept/reject/review in prose but lose the result once it becomes {status, code}, cannot explain brackets/indexing, and may conflate the rule being taught with the container syntax carrying it.
findings.fix: Keep S03 core results as simple strings or visually rendered tables. A small set used solely to demonstrate membership may remain with one microdefinition; defer dict/list/tuple protocols and indexing to S06.
findings.location: opening result-shape paragraph; optional contract; T2-B through T4-B code
findings.prior_knowledge: No collection model beyond a narrow aliasing preview in S02 that was not creditable as mastery.

findings.title: An invariant is a condition required/intended to hold at a specified program or domain boundary; bugs or invalid external inputs can violate it. The current definition sounds like an automatically enforced law of the language.
findings.evidence: The opening says 'un invariante es una promesa que el programa no puede romper' and gives 'el monto nunca es negativo' as an invariant, while the same section validates raw values that can in fact be negative and rejects them.
findings.impact: The learner can conclude that once a statement is called an invariant, invalid values cannot exist, making validation/tests conceptually redundant and obscuring the difference between raw-input constraints and post-validation guarantees.
findings.fix: Define an invariant as 'una condición que declaras que debe cumplirse en una etapa concreta, por ejemplo después de validar; el código y las pruebas detectan cuando no se cumple'. Scope examples explicitly to raw vs accepted data.
findings.location: opening paragraph 4 and T4-A invariant definition
findings.prior_knowledge: No formal invariant concept.

findings.title: The section names and defines a table without teaching the learner how to read one, check coverage of combinations, or translate one row into a branch.
findings.evidence: A learning outcome promises reading a decision table, but theory never renders an actual table with condition columns/rows and actions. It describes the idea, then jumps to prose arrows and match code, even suggesting a dict of examples.
findings.impact: The learner may think a list of code constants or a dict is the decision table and cannot audit whether all business combinations are represented before coding.
findings.fix: Insert one small learner-visible table before match, e.g. code | meaning | status, including default/unknown. Ask the learner to trace each row into if/elif or match.
findings.location: T3-B Tablas de decisión y match/case
findings.prior_knowledge: Ordinary tables are part of ZERO_TECH baseline.

findings.title: The same cause code receives two incompatible statuses in consecutive subtopics with no different domain contract to explain the change.
findings.evidence: T3-A explicitly classifies a region outside the allowlist as review and prints R-FUERA 30 -> review. T3-B then maps the stable code NOT_IN_ALLOWLIST to reject without announcing a policy change, even though it says it is scaling the T3-A motor.
findings.impact: The learner cannot know whether an unknown catalog value is review or reject and may copy either mapping while believing it is the course's canonical policy.
findings.fix: Keep NOT_IN_ALLOWLIST -> review throughout this synthetic policy, or explicitly introduce a new stricter policy/table with a new context and state that the mapping changed by business decision.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner has just learned that unknown and invalid are distinct and that NOT_IN_ALLOWLIST preserves that distinction.

findings.title: S03 violates the exact edge case its previous lesson warned about, turning booleans into ages.
findings.evidence: Both validators use isinstance(edad, int) without excluding bool. S02 explicitly taught that bool is a subtype of int and that business integer validators should use isinstance(x, int) and not isinstance(x, bool). Executing the S03 logic confirms True/False pass the int check; validate_edad_msg(True) returns OK.
findings.impact: The learner can submit True as edad and receive accept/OK in T4-B, learning that the validator is type-safe when it is not.
findings.fix: For domain integer fields where bool is invalid, use if not isinstance(edad, int) or isinstance(edad, bool): BAD_TYPE, and add True/False branch cases.
findings.prior_knowledge: S02's bool/int edge case was explicitly discussed locally even though the broader validation pattern remained partial.

findings.title: The lesson offers two incompatible minimum coverage contracts; the weaker one can miss an entire branch while appearing to satisfy all three statuses.
findings.evidence: T4-A says the professional minimum is at least one example per decision state, but T4-B correctly says one test per branch and gives four paths (None, wrong type, range, OK). Multiple branches can share the same reject state, so one reject example cannot cover them all.
findings.impact: A validator with two reject causes can be tested with only one reject input, leaving the other branch broken while the learner believes the minimum has been met.
findings.fix: Change T4-A to 'at least one example per distinct branch; if several branches share a status, each still needs a case'. Keep accept/reject/review coverage as a secondary check.
findings.location: T4-A paragraph 2 versus T4-B paragraph 2 and learning outcome 8
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic accept/reject/review states and branch model from S03.

findings.title: A visual intended to reduce uncertainty introduces a future control-flow construct before its learner-facing definition.
findings.evidence: The figure caption discusses moving a guard and changing classification before guard clauses or branch ordering are introduced in T2.
findings.impact: The learner sees 'guarda' and ordered branch effects before knowing what a guard is, so the figure cannot perform explanatory work at its current position.
findings.fix: Move S03-guard-order to T2-B after branch order and dead branches are explained; keep T1-A visual-free or use a comparison/membership figure.
findings.location: figure S03-guard-order attached to T1-A Comparaciones y el operador in
findings.prior_knowledge: Only comparisons/membership at this point.

findings.title: The explanation uses the next subtopic's operator to explain the current subtopic's first mental model.
findings.evidence: Chained comparison is explained as equivalent to two comparisons joined by and before and/or are taught in T1-B.
findings.impact: A ZERO_TECH learner must infer what and does precisely in order to understand why 18 <= edad <= 65 works.
findings.fix: Say 'equivale a exigir que se cumplan las dos comparaciones; Python evalúa edad una sola vez' and introduce the and syntax in T1-B.
findings.prior_knowledge: Comparisons yes; Boolean operators no.

findings.title: The novice must decode five future container syntaxes merely to learn the crucial S03 distinction None vs 0.
findings.evidence: The first truthiness list includes (), [], {}, set(), range(0) and mentions while although collections and loop constructs are scheduled later.
findings.impact: Attention shifts from the business distinction to unexplained punctuation and constructors, increasing the chance that the learner memorizes a falsy list instead of learning the policy distinction.
findings.fix: In the core paragraph use False, None, numeric zero and empty string. Add one sentence that empty collections are also falsy and will be revisited in S06; omit while/range examples here.
findings.prior_knowledge: None, bool, numbers and strings are available; collection and range syntax are not.

findings.title: The learner can observe the final operand value yet has no evidence that the right-hand expression was not evaluated.
findings.evidence: The prose defines short-circuit, but the examples '' or 'default', 0 and 99 and 5 and 99 demonstrate operand return values without making skipped evaluation observable.
findings.impact: The learner may equate short-circuit with 'and/or return a convenient operand' and fail to predict why a guard like edad is not None and edad >= 18 safely avoids the second comparison when edad is None.
findings.fix: Add one process worked example in which the second expression would fail if evaluated, e.g. edad=None followed by edad is not None and edad >= 18, and narrate why the right side is skipped.
findings.prior_knowledge: Comparisons, truthiness and the just-introduced and/or operators.

findings.title: A compatibility fallback reopens a settled prerequisite and encourages unsupported runtimes without educational need.
findings.evidence: The callout tells learners on versions earlier than 3.10 to implement the table with if/elif even though the course states it uses Python 3.12 and S01's stated outcome is a 3.12+ environment.
findings.impact: A learner on an old Python can conclude the environment is acceptable and continue accumulating behavior/version differences instead of fixing the S01 setup contract.
findings.fix: State only that match requires the course's Python 3.12 runtime; remove the pre-3.10 fallback from the learner path.
findings.prior_knowledge: Course runtime should already be resolved in S01.

findings.title: The worked example for specification/invariants is harder than the concept because it bundles several unrelated future constructs.
findings.evidence: The invariant example requires isinstance, strip, isdigit, len, dict/list nesting, indexing, for iteration and a function before the learner can focus on what an invariant means. String methods are formally developed later in S07.
findings.impact: The learner can copy a nine-digit validator but cannot explain which line represents the invariant versus incidental normalization/container mechanics.
findings.fix: Use a previously learned scalar rule such as edad is None / 0<=edad<=120 to demonstrate invariant, counterexample and branch tests. Defer string-method validation to S07.
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic strings only; method-call syntax remained PARTIAL after S02.

findings.title: An abbreviation with no learner value at this point creates an external-knowledge obligation.
findings.evidence: The text says stable codes allow metrics and i18n later, but i18n has never been introduced and is not needed to understand actionable messages.
findings.impact: The learner may stop to infer or search for i18n while the actual concept is simply that stable codes can later support translated messages.
findings.fix: Replace i18n with 'traducciones de mensajes' or add 'i18n (internacionalización)' if the abbreviation must be preserved.
findings.prior_knowledge: No internationalization terminology.

findings.title: Fail-closed behavior for a known closed catalog is useful, but 'more secure' is context-dependent and can become operationally wrong when the catalog is incomplete or the policy should review unknown values rather than reject them.
findings.evidence: The lesson says an allowlist is safer than a denylist because forgotten values remain outside, stated as a broad rule before later acknowledging stale/unknown catalog values may require review.
findings.impact: The learner can generalize 'allowlist always safer' to domains where a stale list silently blocks legitimate values or where unknown values require a different state.
findings.fix: Scope the claim: 'En un catálogo cerrado, una allowlist falla cerrado: lo no enumerado no se acepta automáticamente; según la política puede ir a review o reject.'
findings.prior_knowledge: No security-policy model.

findings.title: The lesson still treats internal curriculum labels as meaningful nouns instead of explaining the artifact/case they denote.
findings.evidence: CP-N1-A and CASO-LIM-003 remain learner-facing identifiers without a fresh plain-language expansion. S01/S02 audits already marked the CP/CASO family as unresolved for the zero-tech learner.
findings.impact: The learner can again wonder whether CASO-LIM-003 is a file/tool and what CP-N1-A specifically means in this section.
findings.fix: At first use write 'CP-N1-A, el proyecto acumulativo de captura y calidad de datos del Nivel 1' and 'CASO-LIM-003, el caso sintético de reglas de esta sección'.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner knows there is an accumulating project idea, but the internal IDs were not credited as usable terminology.

findings.title: Curriculum sequence inversion: S03 teaches control flow through functions, loops and collections that the roadmap places in S04-S06.
Core contract drift: invariant definition, NOT_IN_ALLOWLIST status and branch-coverage minimum are internally inconsistent.
Worked examples often demonstrate surrounding syntax rather than isolating the new control-flow concept for a true novice.
The prose confuses asymptotic linear complexity with a one-pass-only design rule.
findings.evidence: The lesson says one pass is enough and that needing two passes probably means information was stored incorrectly. Two sequential passes over n items perform about 2n work and remain O(n); multiple passes can be clearer or intentionally separate concerns.
findings.impact: A learner can reject a clear two-pass O(n) solution as algorithmically wrong or contort code into one pass merely to satisfy a false performance rule.
findings.fix: State that one pass is often sufficient for these counters, but a small fixed number of passes is still O(n); avoid repeated nested rescans when they are unnecessary.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner is learning Big-O for the first time.

findings.title: S04 must iterate over something, but the lesson goes far beyond a bounded iterable preview and makes S06 structures necessary to understand the loop examples.
findings.evidence: Core examples use list literals, lists of dictionaries, dictionary indexing, append, slicing, lists of tuples, set/dict literals, nested structures and indexing even though V3 teaches lists/tuples/dicts/sets/slicing/unpacking formally in S06.
findings.impact: The learner spends attention decoding brackets, keys, append, slicing and nested records instead of predicting how for/while changes state.
findings.fix: Introduce one simple list as an ordered group of values for the sole purpose of iteration, use flat strings/integers in core examples, and defer nested dict/list operations, slicing and structure choice to S06.
findings.location: T1-A, T1-B, T2-A, T3-A, T3-B, T4-A and T4-B code
findings.prior_knowledge: Only a narrow non-creditable aliasing preview from S02; no usable collection model.

findings.title: Unearned syntax is used to explain core S04 outcomes even where Python 3.12 already provides zip(..., strict=True) and where an exception handler is not required to teach an invalid index.
findings.evidence: The lesson defines helper functions with parameters/return, raises ValueError and catches ValueError/IndexError using try/except before S05 teaches functions/return and S09 teaches exceptions.
findings.impact: The learner can understand the loop idea yet be unable to trace why a helper returns, why raise transfers control, or why except runs.
findings.fix: Use top-level loop examples; use zip(..., strict=True) directly; describe the mismatch ValueError without teaching a custom function/handler; move formal reusable helpers to S05 and exception recovery to S09.
findings.location: T1-B zip_strict; T2-B clean_lines; T4-B try/except
findings.prior_knowledge: Functions/return and exceptions remain MENTION_ONLY from earlier leakage and receive no credit.

findings.title: The first rule incorrectly makes 'condition becomes false' the only valid termination mechanism, then the next subtopic contradicts it with break.
findings.evidence: T2-A says a while loop must update state each turn and becomes infinite if the condition never becomes false. T2-B later says while True is legitimate when a reachable break terminates it.
findings.impact: The learner cannot form one stable rule for proving termination and may incorrectly treat every while True as invalid or believe break somehow changes the truth value of True.
findings.fix: Teach one model: a loop needs a reachable exit path—normally the condition eventually becomes false, or a break/return/exception exits it. In S04 core, emphasize condition progress first and introduce break explicitly afterward.
findings.prior_knowledge: First formal while-loop model.

findings.title: The worked example does not demonstrate the safeguard it claims to teach.
findings.evidence: The section promises safeguards against infinite loops and recommends MAX iterations, but its code uses a finite for loop. max_n limits len(kept), not iteration count; if every line is SKIP/blank, the loop can execute every input item regardless of max_n. Execution with 1000 SKIP rows and max_n=2 performs 1000 iterations.
findings.impact: The learner can copy max_n believing it is an iteration safety cap when it only caps accepted items.
findings.fix: Demonstrate a while loop with an explicit iters counter and condition such as while i < len(lines) and iters < MAX_ITERS, then separately demonstrate break/continue on a finite for.
findings.prior_knowledge: for from T1 and while from T2-A.

findings.title: The callout contradicts the central contract of the entire lesson.
findings.evidence: The opening makes attempted rows the denominator and explains why processed rows can bias the rate. T3-A prose repeats attempted rows, but its callout says 'Tasa de error = errores / procesados'.
findings.impact: The learner receives two formulas for the same metric and cannot know which denominator to implement when early failures exist.
findings.fix: Change the callout to 'errores / registros intentados' and define attempted/processed once if the course needs both terms.
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic arithmetic; denominator semantics are the section's main business concept.

findings.title: The roadmap asks for readable comprehensions, but the example makes three different container kinds and nested record access prerequisites to reading the syntax.
findings.evidence: The first comprehension example simultaneously uses a list of dictionaries, dictionary indexing, a list comprehension, set comprehension, dict comprehension, sorted(), and later dict lookup. S06 has not yet taught those structures.
findings.impact: A learner cannot tell which parts constitute the comprehension versus which parts are dictionary/set syntax, so the intended compact loop/filter transformation remains opaque.
findings.fix: Teach one list comprehension over a simple flat list first, e.g. positivos = [m for m in montos if m > 0]. Defer dict/set comprehensions and nested records to S06.
findings.prior_knowledge: for/if from S03-S04; no usable dict/set model.

findings.title: A known-bad prior mental model is imported into debugging as though mastered.
findings.evidence: The trace paragraph tells the learner to locate the first frame that 'rompe el invariante'. The effective S03 ledger marks invariant MISCONCEPTION_RISK because S03 defined it as something the program cannot break. S04 does not repair the term before depending on it.
findings.impact: The learner can wonder how a trace can ever show an invariant being broken if an invariant was defined as something the program cannot break.
findings.fix: At first reuse say 'la condición que esperabas conservar (el invariante)' and explicitly note that a bug can violate it; the trace helps find the first violation.
findings.prior_knowledge: Only USABLE prior concepts may be assumed; invariant is not one of them.

findings.title: The wrong operation is blamed for the exception.
findings.evidence: The lesson says 'range(len(xs)+1) explota con IndexError'. range(len(xs)+1) is valid and yields 0 through len(xs); IndexError occurs only when that last index is used to access xs[len(xs)].
findings.impact: The learner can expect constructing/iterating the range itself to fail and cannot localize an IndexError to sequence access.
findings.fix: Say 'si usas for i in range(len(xs)+1) para acceder xs[i], la última vuelta intenta xs[len(xs)] y ese acceso lanza IndexError'.
findings.prior_knowledge: First off-by-one debugging model.

findings.title: The learner-facing identity uses an ambiguous domain adjective and internal/English labels instead of stating the actual skill: iterating over batches and producing reliable summaries.
findings.evidence: The title uses 'resúmenes transaccionales' without defining transaccional, while examples span intake rows, sensors, enrollments and transactions. The tagline uses 'comprehensions' and 'Client Intake CP-N1-A' before plain-language expansion.
findings.impact: A learner can expect database transaction semantics or a finance-only lesson and cannot infer what CP-N1-A denotes.
findings.fix: Prefer 'Iteración y resúmenes por lote' and expand CP-N1-A once in plain language; translate or microdefine comprehension at first meaningful use.
findings.prior_knowledge: No transaction-processing or internal curriculum-ID vocabulary.

findings.title: The contrast conflates 'one program execution for many records' with 'not processing records one at a time'.
findings.evidence: A batch processor is defined as a program that 'recorre muchos registros en un solo pase, no uno por uno'. A normal for loop over a batch still handles successive records one by one inside one execution/pass.
findings.impact: The learner can infer that batch processing implies simultaneous processing and later misclassify a sequential loop as not being batch processing.
findings.fix: Say that batch processing handles many records in one execution, usually visiting them successively inside a loop.
findings.prior_knowledge: No batch-processing model.

findings.title: A fallback for unsupported course runtimes creates extra functions/exceptions and reopens version ambiguity.
findings.evidence: S04 repeatedly frames strict zip as Python 3.10+ and supplies a manual compatibility helper although the course runtime is intended to be Python 3.12.
findings.impact: The learner can infer that the course expects multiple unsupported Python versions and cannot tell whether to use the built-in strict option or the helper.
findings.fix: Assume the canonical Python 3.12 runtime and teach zip(..., strict=True) directly; remove the compatibility helper from core theory.
findings.prior_knowledge: The course should inherit one canonical runtime contract from S01.

findings.title: A common risk is turned into an absolute hardware claim.
findings.evidence: The callout states that an infinite loop in production 'agota CPU y bloquea el lote'. Infinite loops can block progress and consume resources, but a loop that sleeps or waits for I/O does not necessarily exhaust CPU.
findings.impact: The learner can use CPU saturation as a diagnostic criterion for infinite loops and miss loops that are stuck while waiting or sleeping.
findings.fix: Say an unintended infinite loop can prevent progress and may consume CPU or other resources depending on what its body does.
findings.prior_knowledge: No operating-systems performance model.

findings.title: A new decision syntax is embedded in the line whose denominator behavior is supposed to be the learning focus.
findings.evidence: The expression 'n_reject / n_total if n_total else None' introduces Python's conditional-expression syntax without explaining it; S03 taught if statements, not this expression form.
findings.impact: The learner can memorize the one-line pattern without knowing which branch is selected or why None appears for an empty batch.
findings.fix: Use an explicit if/else block already learned in S03, or add a microdefinition only if conditional expressions are intentionally introduced here.
findings.prior_knowledge: if/elif/else statements are USABLE; conditional expressions are not.

findings.title: A trace mismatch can originate in the branch condition, validator output, test data, state update, display code or counter. The evidence given does not isolate one cause.
findings.evidence: The prose says that if a trace does not match the print, the bug is in state update, and if it does not match the summary the bug is in the counter, not the S03 validator.
findings.impact: The learner can stop investigating the validator or condition because the lesson told them the counter must be at fault.
findings.fix: Use the trace to locate the first divergent state, then inspect the condition/update that produced that divergence; do not predeclare which component is innocent.
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic tracing only.

findings.title: The term is stretched from index/count mistakes to every inclusive/exclusive policy error.
findings.evidence: The lesson labels >= versus > in business thresholds as 'off-by-one de negocio'. This is a boundary/inclusivity error; it is only literally off-by-one for discrete integer boundaries where the threshold differs by one accepted value.
findings.impact: The learner can call any boundary-policy mistake off-by-one and lose the useful distinction between indexing errors and business-rule boundary errors.
findings.fix: Call >= versus > a 'boundary/inclusivity error'; then note that for integer counts it can resemble an off-by-one error.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner is forming the term off-by-one for the first time.

findings.title: The curriculum's internal identifiers remain part of explanatory prose rather than labels attached to an already-understood artifact.
findings.evidence: CP-N1-A and CASO-LIM-004 continue to appear as learner-facing identifiers without a stable plain-language expansion at first use.
findings.impact: The learner can still treat CP-N1-A/CASO-LIM-004 as tools, files or commands instead of course artifacts.
findings.fix: Expand once: 'CP-N1-A, el proyecto acumulativo de captura y calidad de datos del Nivel 1' and 'CASO-LIM-004, el caso sintético de procesamiento por lotes'.
findings.location: tagline, opening callout and optional contract
findings.prior_knowledge: Earlier occurrences were explicitly not credited as understood.

findings.title: Buffer is central to the while example but is presented as implementation vocabulary rather than a simple temporary collection of pending lines.
findings.evidence: The lesson says browser demos simulate a 'buffer de líneas' without explaining buffer; pipeline/tests/CSV are also used as process labels before their dedicated sections.
findings.impact: The learner may search for a special Python buffer type or fail to understand where the lines came from and why an index advances through them.
findings.fix: Say 'una lista que simula las líneas pendientes de leer' and keep pipeline/CSV references context-only or replace them with 'proceso de datos' until their real sections.
findings.prior_knowledge: No buffering or data-pipeline architecture.

findings.title: Roadmap S04 gate says the final script processes records via stdin/stdout, while roadmap S10 explicitly teaches stdin/stdout/CLI. Theory S04 simulates a browser buffer and does not teach stdin/stdout. Decide whether S04 needs only batch-loop semantics or a bounded stdin/stdout micro-model.
Exact live rendered order/visual relationship of figures, callouts and code could not be verified because the public page fetch is blocked in the current environment.
Future structures/functions/exceptions are used as scaffolding for first-time iteration concepts.
Several core technical rules are internally false or contradictory: one-pass O(n), while termination, denominator vocabulary and range/IndexError causality.
Worked examples frequently demonstrate a more complex implementation surface than the specific loop concept they are supposed to isolate.
A function contract includes behavioral guarantees, not only the visible signature or input/output shape. Internal code can change without changing the signature and still violate the postcondition.
findings.evidence: The caption says implementation is inside the box and 'Cambiar el cuerpo sin tocar los bordes es libre'.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can believe that any body-only change is a safe refactor as long as the parameters and return shape stay unchanged.
findings.fix: Change the caption to say the implementation may change only while preserving the contract: preconditions, outputs, errors and observable effects.
findings.prior_knowledge: This is the learner's first legitimate function-contract lesson.

findings.title: The example intended to teach definition/call/return requires the learner to decode several unrelated transformations before they can trace the function boundary.
findings.evidence: The first worked function uses raw.strip().split(), join(), title(), annotations and a second no-return function while string methods are formally S07 and function mechanics are new here.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can reproduce normalize_nombre while still being unable to explain when a def body runs, how raw receives an argument or how return hands a value back.
findings.fix: Start T1-A with a one-operation function whose body uses already-earned syntax, trace definition -> call -> parameter binding -> return, then introduce normalize_nombre after the function model exists.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner can use basic values, decisions and loops but has not earned the string-method toolkit.

findings.title: The roadmap requires safe defaults before it teaches the mutable structures that make the default bug understandable; the lesson uses those structures without a bounded micro-model.
findings.evidence: The key safe-default outcome is taught using [] lists, append(), shared-object mutation and list-return behavior although S06 is the first collection lesson and the prior ledger does not credit list mutation mastery.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can memorize 'use None' without understanding that one mutable default object is created once and then changed across calls.
findings.fix: Add an explicit micro-model: a list is a changeable container; the default object is created once at def time; append changes that same object. Keep the detailed collection mechanics for S06.
findings.prior_knowledge: No operational list/dict mutation model.

findings.title: The lesson does not distinguish an assumed caller obligation from a runtime validation performed by the callee or by an external boundary.
findings.evidence: Prose defines a precondition as what must be true before calling; the figure says the precondition 'se comprueba antes de tocar nada'; the example states 'Pre: raw es str' but performs no explicit type check and would raise AttributeError for None/int.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner cannot tell whether every documented precondition must be checked inside the function, is automatically enforced by Python, or is merely required of callers.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: a precondition states what callers must provide; it may be assumed inside trusted core code or explicitly validated at an untrusted boundary. Make the figure say 'declarar/validar según el boundary', not that every precondition is automatically checked.
findings.prior_knowledge: No prior formal design-by-contract model.

findings.title: The worked example violates the section's own gradual-hints rule and makes type syntax plus tuple semantics prerequisites for understanding domain errors.
findings.evidence: The prose says not to overload S05 with advanced generics, then immediately imports Optional and Tuple and uses Tuple[bool, Optional[int], Optional[str]], a three-field tuple result, before S06 teaches tuples and structured collections.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can interpret type hints as a nested mini-language they must master immediately and cannot distinguish the function's domain-error idea from its result-container syntax.
findings.fix: Keep T2-B examples to simple public annotations such as raw: str -> str; postpone Optional/Tuple result protocols to S06 or introduce one bounded str | None form only when it is genuinely needed.
findings.prior_knowledge: Simple annotations such as x: str -> str only.

findings.title: S05 legitimately needs to state domain-error behavior, but it asks the learner to trace exception control flow without first teaching what raise interrupts, what except catches, or where execution resumes.
findings.evidence: normalize_email raises ValueError and theory demonstrates try/except; parse_edad also uses try/except, while the roadmap reserves exception/recovery mechanics for S09.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can memorize try/except as boilerplate around validation without understanding why the normal return path is skipped.
findings.fix: Either give a tightly bounded micro-model of raise/ValueError sufficient for function contracts and defer recovery patterns to S09, or use explicit result values in S05 and postpone try/except demonstrations.
findings.prior_knowledge: No usable exception-flow model from the effective ledger.

findings.title: The learner must understand a future data structure to see what the orchestrator returns and how composition preserves each helper's result.
findings.evidence: The canonical composition example returns a dict from normalize_record, constructs a dict literal and uses that container as the core representation before S06 teaches dictionaries.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can understand each helper separately but lose the composition model exactly when the outputs are packaged in unexplained dict syntax.
findings.fix: Demonstrate composition first with a simple returned string/value pair expressed separately; introduce record dictionaries only after S06 or provide a bounded explicit preview if the roadmap is revised.
findings.prior_knowledge: No usable dict model.

findings.title: The lesson conflates injecting a transformation strategy with injecting I/O and never shows how external reading/writing is supplied to or kept outside the pure core.
findings.evidence: T3-B explains that I/O belongs at the boundary, but the promised injection example passes a normalizer function as norm=normalize_telefono and the callout calls that 'inyección'; it does not inject any input/output dependency.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can finish S05 believing that passing any function argument counts as I/O injection and still hard-code open()/print() around business logic.
findings.fix: Either rename the outcome/topic to dependency injection if that is the intended skill, or show one tiny boundary function that receives an I/O callable while the normalizer remains pure.
findings.location: learning outcome 'inyectar I/O en el borde' + S05-T3-B
findings.prior_knowledge: Functions are now in scope; I/O separation is a declared outcome.

findings.title: The example intended to make f(f(x)) == f(x) visible hides the transformation behind new syntax and new text rules.
findings.evidence: The main idempotence example computes digits with ''.join(ch for ch in raw if ch.isdigit()), combining a generator expression and string-method semantics that have not been taught as usable concepts.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner may verify the printed equality but be unable to predict why the first normalization produced that value or whether applying it twice should remain stable.
findings.fix: Demonstrate idempotence first with a normalizer whose transformation is already transparent to the learner; move generator-expression/string-method implementation to the later text lesson.
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic for loops are usable; generator expressions and string-method validation are not.

findings.title: The example claims configuration is captured by prefix but one major policy decision remains hidden and Peru-specific inside the closure.
findings.evidence: The prose presents make_phone_normalizer(prefix) as country-configurable, but the inner function hard-codes startswith('51') and d[2:] regardless of the supplied prefix. Execution with make_phone_normalizer('+1') duplicates +1 for an already +1 input and strips a leading 51 even though +1 was requested.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can believe the factory is generic by country when changing the prefix alone does not change its country-code stripping logic.
findings.fix: Use a closure example whose behavior depends only on the captured prefix, or pass the digits-to-strip/country policy explicitly as configuration too.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner is using a closure to understand captured configuration.

findings.title: The worked example does not establish a pre-refactor green baseline and therefore cannot demonstrate that behavior was preserved across the change.
findings.evidence: The file defines normalize_email v1, defines _examples, then redefines normalize_email v2 and calls _examples only afterward. Python resolves the global normalize_email when _examples executes, so every assertion runs against v2; v1 is never tested in that run.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can believe tests prove a refactor preserved behavior even when only the final implementation was ever exercised.
findings.fix: Run the same example assertions before redefining/refactoring the function and again afterward, or keep v1/v2 under distinct names and compare both against the same examples.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner is supposed to see tests fixed before and after a refactor.

findings.title: The real hazard is a mutable default that the function mutates; lists and dicts are examples, not the complete category. Mutable class instances can create the same problem.
findings.evidence: The rule is repeatedly phrased as 'nunca una lista o un diccionario' / 'nunca uses lista/dict mutable como default'.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can conclude that a set or other mutable object is automatically safe merely because it is not a list or dict.
findings.fix: Say 'evita objetos mutables como listas o diccionarios cuando la función puede modificarlos; usa None y crea un objeto nuevo dentro'.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner is forming the reusable rule for safe defaults.

findings.title: These are true facts but they are not needed for the T1-A outcome and introduce future collection/callback concepts before the basic call trace is stable.
findings.evidence: Immediately after first defining call/return, the lesson introduces first-class functions, storing them in lists, returning functions and callbacks.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can spend working memory on what a callback or function-as-value is instead of distinguishing definition, call and return.
findings.fix: Move first-class/callback material to T4-A when closures/factories are introduced, or to an optional note after the core function model.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner is still constructing the first function-call model.

findings.title: Runtime behavior comes from code, but intended contract is not automatically whatever the current implementation happens to do. A mismatch is a defect that requires deciding which artifact is wrong.
findings.evidence: The callout says 'Si el docstring y el código discrepan, gana el código'.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can silently rewrite documentation to match a buggy implementation instead of treating the discrepancy as evidence requiring resolution.
findings.fix: Replace with 'si discrepan, hay un defecto: ejecuta/consulta la especificación y corrige el artefacto que no representa la política acordada'.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner is being taught that a docstring expresses a contract.

findings.title: Purity does not determine whether errors should be exceptions or result values, and a batch can catch per-record exceptions without aborting the whole batch.
findings.evidence: The callout prescribes 'raise para API internas puras; tupla u objeto de resultado cuando el lote no debe abortar'.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can infer a false one-to-one rule between internal/pure functions and exceptions, then design inconsistent APIs when callers have different recovery needs.
findings.fix: State that either pattern can be valid; choose one explicit contract based on how callers must recover, and use it consistently within the module.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner is choosing an error contract for the first time.

findings.title: Lambda is not required for any S05 outcome and adds a second function syntax plus substitution semantics at the exact point where I/O injection is already underexplained.
findings.evidence: The callout introduces lambda syntax while the section's own function model and dependency-injection idea are still being learned.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can treat lambda as required for testing/injection or confuse it with a fundamentally different kind of function.
findings.fix: Remove lambda from core S05 theory or put it in an optional later note after closures/factories.
findings.prior_knowledge: Named def functions only.

findings.title: The closure mechanism is buried under unrelated phone-normalization rules.
findings.evidence: The closure example simultaneously uses isdigit(), startswith(), len(), slicing d[2:], nested defs and country normalization. Slicing is S06 and the text-method toolkit is S07.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can fail to identify which value is remembered by the closure because most visible lines are about text parsing rather than scope.
findings.fix: Use a minimal factory such as make_prefixer(prefix) whose inner function returns prefix + raw, then trace raw/prefix/global separately.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner needs only enough syntax to see Local -> Enclosing -> Global -> Builtin and a captured prefix.

findings.title: The strong earlier statement is broader than the evidence and is only corrected several paragraphs later.
findings.evidence: The paragraph says that if asserts stay green, 'la conducta se preservó'. Paragraph 5 later correctly limits this by saying green proves only what the examples cover.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can temporarily form the rule 'all green examples prove unchanged behavior', overlooking uncovered inputs or side effects.
findings.fix: Change the first statement to 'si siguen verdes, preservaste la conducta que esos ejemplos cubren'; keep the later caveat.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner is forming a first model of regression evidence.

findings.title: The learner sees the delivery contract but not a complete learner-facing model of that contract inside theory.
findings.evidence: The lesson says closing S05 means four normalizers plus an orchestrator with docstring/hints/idempotence demonstrated, but theory's normalize_record combines only nombre/email and has no docstring; normalize_direccion is never implemented in a theory code block.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can reach practice knowing the names of four policies but without a canonical example showing the full orchestrator boundary promised by the lesson.
findings.fix: Either narrow the theory callout to the patterns actually modeled, or add one compact final reference example of the four-function orchestrator after the concepts have been taught.
findings.location: opening callout/optional criterion + T3-A canonical orchestrator
findings.prior_knowledge: Theory should give enough canonical evidence before practice, without having to inspect You Do.

findings.title: Assert is shown as evidence for refactoring without delimiting it as a development/example mechanism rather than production validation.
findings.evidence: S05 promotes assert as executable examples but does not locally remind learners that Python -O removes assert statements; prior S03 testing knowledge was not credited as USABLE.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can reuse assert as the only enforcement of a business precondition and assume it always executes.
findings.fix: Add a one-sentence boundary: asserts are development checks/examples and can be removed under python -O; do not use them as the only production validation of external input.
findings.prior_knowledge: No stable testing/assert mental model.

findings.title: The learner is repeatedly asked to treat internal codes as meaningful nouns.
findings.evidence: CP-N1-B and CASO-LIM-005 remain learner-facing internal identifiers without stable first-use expansion in plain language.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a learner can recognize the labels but not explain whether they denote a project, gate, dataset, exercise or software component.
