findings.fix: Separate the course's pre-1.0 policy from SemVer 1.x rules; define exactly how 0.y.z changes are versioned before declaring 1.0.0.

findings.title: Due to this problem, a Windows learner can think stdin piping is unavailable or that their shell is wrong when cat is not the documented com…
findings.evidence: The only shell example uses cat data.json, while S01 explicitly supports Windows/PowerShell as a first-class path.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a Windows learner can think stdin piping is unavailable or that their shell is wrong when cat is not the documented command for their environment.
findings.fix: Label Unix/macOS and PowerShell examples separately, or use a platform-neutral conceptual pipe plus both concrete commands.

findings.title: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can lose an explicit clear/disable value from a configuration source and believe it was absent.
findings.evidence: Prose says None in flags means 'not passed', but code filters None from file_cfg and env_cfg too. That silently treats explicit None in every layer as missing.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can lose an explicit clear/disable value from a configuration source and believe it was absent.
findings.fix: Apply the 'None means not passed' rule only to the layer whose parser uses that sentinel, or represent absence with omitted keys/a dedicated sentinel.

findings.title: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can let jobs='4' override jobs=1 and later hit type-dependent behavior while believing the precede…
findings.evidence: env_cfg is shown as an ordinary typed dict even though Python os.environ keys and values are strings. Numeric/boolean settings require explicit parsing before merge/validation.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can let jobs='4' override jobs=1 and later hit type-dependent behavior while believing the precedence merge preserved the configuration type.
findings.fix: State that environment values arrive as strings and parse each supported key into its contract type before merging.

findings.title: The learner believes changing dict to dataclass automatically validates runtime types and required semantic values.
findings.evidence: The lesson says a named type has fixed boxes whose required fields cannot be left empty and prevents one field being text in one function and numeric in another. The first dataclass does not enforce type hints or non-empty values at runtime.
findings.impact: The learner believes changing dict to dataclass automatically validates runtime types and required semantic values.
findings.fix: Separate named structure, static annotations and runtime validation; state that dataclass/type hints alone do not enforce domain validity.

findings.title: The learner can instantiate a dataclass but cannot explain where instance attributes come from or how a normal class initializes state.
findings.evidence: The first class example starts with @dataclass, generated __init__/__repr__, field and default_factory before showing the basic class-instance-state-method mechanism or self.
findings.impact: The learner can instantiate a dataclass but cannot explain where instance attributes come from or how a normal class initializes state.
findings.fix: Show one tiny ordinary class with __init__, self and one method before introducing @dataclass as generated boilerplate.

findings.title: The learner cannot tell which ClientRecord fields are actually required and can construct an object that violates the stated domain contract…
findings.evidence: jobRelevance defines a valid client as having email and DNI; ClientRecord gives emails an empty default, validates only client_id/document_id, and does not validate full_name.
findings.impact: The learner cannot tell which ClientRecord fields are actually required and can construct an object that violates the stated domain contract.
findings.fix: Choose and state one client invariant set, then enforce every required field consistently in the canonical class.

findings.title: The learner equates constructor validation with preservation of an invariant for the object's whole lifetime.
findings.evidence: Invariants are defined as conditions the object always satisfies, but ClientRecord is mutable. After construction c.document_id = '' leaves a live object violating the validated rule.
findings.impact: The learner equates constructor validation with preservation of an invariant for the object's whole lifetime.
findings.fix: Either freeze/protect invariant-bearing fields or define the rule honestly as construction-time validation and teach how allowed mutations preserve validity.

findings.title: The learner sees an explicit invariant violated by the canonical example without any failure.
findings.evidence: Opening says CaseFile cannot sustain a relationship without at least one RelationshipEvidence; composition.py constructs CaseFile(entity=ResolvedEntity('E1')) with evidences=[] as valid.
findings.impact: The learner sees an explicit invariant violated by the canonical example without any failure.
findings.fix: Remove that claimed invariant or require evidence at construction/use an explicit draft state.

findings.title: The learner reaches practice without a worked model for one quarter of the required domain types and its monetary invariant.
findings.evidence: The gate promises four explicit types ClientRecord, ResolvedEntity, Transaction and RelationshipEvidence, but theory never provides a canonical Transaction class implementation; Transaction exists only in prose.
findings.impact: The learner reaches practice without a worked model for one quarter of the required domain types and its monetary invariant.
findings.fix: Add a minimal Transaction dataclass with amount/currency validation in theory.

findings.title: The learner believes adding a property protects underlying mutable public state or enforces authorization.
findings.evidence: The prose says @property exposes derived fields without dangerous external mutation and raw email remains in an internal field for authorized boundaries, but emails is a public mutable list and can be appended/replaced directly.
findings.impact: The learner believes adding a property protects underlying mutable public state or enforces authorization.
findings.fix: State that property controls only that property access; make sensitive state private/read-only by design or return immutable/copy views and define authorization outside the property.

findings.title: The learner treats isinstance(store, EntityStore) as runtime interface validation.
findings.evidence: The prose implies @runtime_checkable isinstance verifies the Protocol contract at runtime. Python documents that runtime-checkable protocols check attribute presence only, not method signatures or annotated types. A WrongStore with wrong get/save signatures still passes isinstance.
findings.impact: The learner treats isinstance(store, EntityStore) as runtime interface validation.
findings.fix: Teach Protocol primarily as a static structural contract; label runtime_checkable as a shallow presence check.

findings.title: The port erases the domain types exactly at the architecture boundary where the lesson claims named types matter.
findings.evidence: After teaching named domain types, EntityStore.get/save revert to Optional[dict]/dict and FakeStore stores anonymous dictionaries.
findings.impact: The port erases the domain types exactly at the architecture boundary where the lesson claims named types matter.
findings.fix: Define the port in terms of a domain type such as ResolvedEntity or ClientRecord; use DTO dicts only at an explicitly named serialization adapter.

findings.title: The learner cannot see structural substitution or swap FakeStore/real adapter without changing the service contract.
findings.evidence: ClientService is typed directly to InMemoryClientRepository rather than EntityStore, and the repository get/save signatures use ClientRecord while the earlier EntityStore Protocol uses dict. The taught port is not used by the service it was supposed to decouple.
findings.impact: The learner cannot see structural substitution or swap FakeStore/real adapter without changing the service contract.
findings.fix: Use one Protocol whose methods operate on the same domain type, then annotate ClientService(repo: ClientRepository).

findings.title: The learner receives two incompatible meanings of where serialization belongs.
findings.evidence: The prose says to_dict/from_dict live at the serialization boundary and are not mixed into business entities; code defines ClientRecord.to_dict on the entity itself and provides no from_dict boundary object/function.
findings.impact: The learner receives two incompatible meanings of where serialization belongs.
findings.fix: Either explicitly choose entity serialization methods and defend that tradeoff, or move mapping to named adapter functions/classes outside the entity.

findings.title: The learner learns that later examples may silently discard earlier invariants while retaining the same class name.
findings.evidence: ClientRecord is redefined without validate/__post_init__. ClientService.register('', '', '', '') constructs and stores an invalid object despite T1-B's invariant contract.
findings.impact: The learner learns that later examples may silently discard earlier invariants while retaining the same class name.
findings.fix: Reuse one canonical domain model across subtopics instead of redefining weakened versions.

findings.title: The learner sees PASS while none of the central validity rules are executable in the class under test.
findings.evidence: Prose says tests verify finiteness, range, canonical pair and no verdicts. The test redefines RelationshipEvidence without __post_init__ and tests only one valid score plus two hasattr checks. Non-finite, out-of-range and reversed pairs still construct successfully in that class.
findings.impact: The learner sees PASS while none of the central validity rules are executable in the class under test.
findings.fix: Import/reuse the canonical RelationshipEvidence and add negative tests for reversed/equal ids, NaN/inf and scores outside [0,1].

findings.title: The learner recognizes labels without knowing whether they denote a paradigm, project increment, system, process or interface boundary.
findings.evidence: OOP is not expanded at first use; CP-N1-C, matching/familiaridad and puertos testeables appear before a stable learner-facing definition.
findings.impact: The learner recognizes labels without knowing whether they denote a paradigm, project increment, system, process or interface boundary.
findings.fix: Expand Programación Orientada a Objetos (OOP) and CP-N1-C once; define matching/familiaridad by function and delay port terminology until Protocol.

findings.title: Boundary value 0 has two different contracts.
findings.evidence: Opening says Transaction amount cannot be negative, which permits zero; T1-B later says amount must be positive and rejects amount <= 0.
findings.impact: Boundary value 0 has two different contracts.
findings.fix: Choose non-negative or strictly positive and use it everywhere, including tests.

findings.title: The learner treats frozen as deep immutability.
findings.evidence: frozen=True is described as preventing object mutation. Dataclasses emulate read-only field assignment; mutable objects stored inside a frozen dataclass can still mutate.
findings.impact: The learner treats frozen as deep immutability.
findings.fix: Say frozen prevents normal reassignment/deletion of fields, not mutation inside mutable field values; prefer immutable field types for hashable value objects.

findings.title: The learner may persist or compare Python hash values as stable entity identifiers across runs.
findings.evidence: Hash is glossed as a fixed number. Python salts str hashes, so a dataclass hash based on entity_id strings can differ across interpreter processes even while remaining valid for local sets/dicts.
findings.impact: The learner may persist or compare Python hash values as stable entity identifiers across runs.
findings.fix: Clarify that hash must stay stable while an object is used in a hashed collection during a run; it is not a persistent identifier.

findings.title: The learner can add an equivalent automatic verdict under another method name and still pass the supposed ethics gate.
findings.evidence: Absence checks for two exact method names are presented as protection of the ethical product boundary.
findings.impact: The learner can add an equivalent automatic verdict under another method name and still pass the supposed ethics gate.
findings.fix: Describe these asserts as narrow API regression checks; protect the broader boundary through documented prohibited capabilities plus review/tests of public outputs.

findings.title: The learner must distinguish multiple abstraction mechanisms before the basic class/object/composition model is stable.
findings.evidence: In the first canonical OOP lesson, the core composition/Protocol sequence also introduces subtype, mixin, MRO, ABC, YAGNI, duck typing, static checking, runtime_checkable and adapters.
findings.impact: The learner must distinguish multiple abstraction mechanisms before the basic class/object/composition model is stable.
findings.fix: Keep core to class-instance, composition and one Protocol port; move mixin/MRO/ABC comparison to optional extension.

findings.title: The learner can confuse synthetic lookalike data with actual PII classification and mistake a prose label for access control.
findings.evidence: Synthetic email/name examples are called 'PII sintética (información personal identificable de mentira)' and the prose invokes 'export legal/backoffice autorizado' without defining any real authorization model.
findings.impact: The learner can confuse synthetic lookalike data with actual PII classification and mistake a prose label for access control.
findings.fix: Say 'datos sintéticos con forma de datos personales, que no corresponden a personas reales'; treat authorization as an external system responsibility.

findings.title: The learner can read ': str' as runtime admission control.
findings.evidence: Type hints are described as telling the verifier which values a field admits, but prior type-hint mastery was not creditable and the local text does not restate that Python does not enforce these annotations at runtime.
findings.impact: The learner can read ': str' as runtime admission control.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: annotations help readers/type checkers; runtime validity still requires explicit validation when the domain needs it.

findings.title: The structural-typing idea is buried beneath unrelated annotation compatibility syntax.
findings.evidence: The first Protocol example simultaneously adds from __future__ import annotations, legacy Dict/Optional forms, Protocol, runtime_checkable and runtime isinstance despite the course targeting Python 3.12+.
findings.impact: The structural-typing idea is buried beneath unrelated annotation compatibility syntax.
findings.fix: Use Python 3.12 forms (dict[str, T], T | None), omit future annotations unless needed, and demonstrate static Protocol conformance before runtime_checkable.

findings.title: The learner can classify every 4xx as malformed request while simultaneously memorizing 429 as a server error, producing incompatible status…
findings.evidence: Opening says 'los 400 significan que el pedido estaba mal formulado' and then treats 429 as a server-side transient example. T1-A later correctly makes 429 a special retryable 4xx under course policy.
findings.impact: The learner can classify every 4xx as malformed request while simultaneously memorizing 429 as a server error, producing incompatible status-to-action logic.
findings.fix: Teach status classes as broad categories, then classify action by specific status: 400 malformed/bad request, 401 auth, 404 missing, 429 rate limit, 503 unavailable.

findings.title: The learner can reason about a fake status object yet still cannot construct a request, pass headers/timeout, receive bytes, decode the body…
findings.evidence: Outcome promises consuming synchronous HTTP APIs, headers, timeout and response handling; theory code only constructs MockResponse objects and a local dictionary. urllib/urlopen is mentioned but never demonstrated.
findings.impact: The learner can reason about a fake status object yet still cannot construct a request, pass headers/timeout, receive bytes, decode the body, or map network exceptions in a real synchronous adapter.
findings.fix: Add one minimal stdlib adapter around urllib.request with a transport seam/fake so the mechanism is visible without requiring live internet.

findings.title: The learner reaches practice knowing the words retry/backoff but with no executable model of when an attempt repeats, how long it waits, or…
findings.evidence: T1-B promises retry/backoff, Retry-After and max_retries; the canonical code implements pagination and increments a delay counter only. No should_retry, attempts, backoff schedule or Retry-After handling exists.
findings.impact: The learner reaches practice knowing the words retry/backoff but with no executable model of when an attempt repeats, how long it waits, or when it stops.
findings.fix: Add a deterministic bounded retry loop with explicit retryable statuses, attempt counter, Retry-After/backoff delay and terminal failure path.

findings.title: A learner can wrap a non-idempotent POST/write in the same timeout retry policy and duplicate side effects when the first attempt succeeded…
findings.evidence: The section introduces GET/POST and then describes retrying timeouts/statuses generically even though S09 left idempotency MISCONCEPTION_RISK. It never limits automatic retry to safe/idempotent operations or explains how a POST becomes safely retryable.
findings.impact: A learner can wrap a non-idempotent POST/write in the same timeout retry policy and duplicate side effects when the first attempt succeeded but the response was lost.
findings.fix: State that the canonical retry demo is a GET/read; do not automatically retry non-idempotent writes unless the operation contract/idempotency key makes repetition safe.

findings.title: The learner can infer that putting a token-like value into source is the normal way to populate an environment variable, exactly the mechani…
findings.evidence: Prose says never hardcode or use a demo token pasted into code; canonical code immediately executes os.environ['API_TOKEN'] = 'demo-token-not-real'.
findings.impact: The learner can infer that putting a token-like value into source is the normal way to populate an environment variable, exactly the mechanism the paragraph warns against.
findings.fix: Inject a synthetic environment mapping into get_token for the deterministic demo, while showing that real os.environ is populated outside source code.

findings.title: If two identities can see different representations at the same URL, a learner can reuse one principal's cached response for another princip…
findings.evidence: The authenticated-adapter subtopic caches GET responses using sha256(url) only. Authentication identity/scope/tenant is absent from the key and cache policy.
findings.impact: If two identities can see different representations at the same URL, a learner can reuse one principal's cached response for another principal.
findings.fix: Cache only explicitly public/shared resources or include a non-secret authorization scope/tenant identifier in the cache key; never include the raw bearer token.

findings.title: A green static fixture test can be mistaken for evidence that the provider has not drifted.
findings.evidence: Prose says a provider field rename makes the fixture-based contract test fail before production. assert_contract only inspects a fixed local payload; it has no connection to the provider's current schema.
findings.impact: A green static fixture test can be mistaken for evidence that the provider has not drifted.
findings.fix: Distinguish local adapter regression tests from provider/sandbox contract checks; static fixtures catch code regressions only after the expected contract/fixture is updated from trusted provider evidence.

findings.title: The learner cannot implement the actual causal boundary failure -> fallback -> provenance because the demo models a manual mode switch inste…
findings.evidence: Prose says 5xx/network failure triggers precomputed fallback. Code merely switches on a caller-supplied online boolean; no request failure/status causes the branch and no failure reason is carried.
findings.impact: The learner cannot implement the actual causal boundary failure -> fallback -> provenance because the demo models a manual mode switch instead.
findings.fix: Use a fake online adapter that raises/returns 503, catch/classify that failure at the boundary, select the offline dataset, and record fallback_reason.

findings.title: The first real external boundary bypasses the named domain model and reinforces the pre-S11 habit of allowing unvalidated dictionaries to ci…
findings.evidence: S11 is a required prerequisite, but canonical S12 theory never references ClientRecord, ResolvedEntity, Transaction or RelationshipEvidence. External JSON, cache bodies, SQL rows and evidence continue as anonymous dicts/tuples.
findings.impact: The first real external boundary bypasses the named domain model and reinforces the pre-S11 habit of allowing unvalidated dictionaries to circulate through the system.
findings.fix: Show the complete boundary: external DTO/dict -> explicit validation/parsing -> canonical S11 domain constructor -> repository mapping.

findings.title: The learner can collapse client identity and resolved-entity identity, destroying the layer separation that CP-N1-C relies on.
findings.evidence: Paragraph says clients/transactions/evidence names are aligned with S11. DDL creates clients(id,name) and evidence(entity_id), then inserts evidence.entity_id='C001' and joins it directly to clients.id. S11 distinguishes ClientRecord client_id C... from ResolvedEntity entity_id E... and RelationshipEvidence left_id/right_id.
findings.impact: The learner can collapse client identity and resolved-entity identity, destroying the layer separation that CP-N1-C relies on.
findings.fix: Either map evidence explicitly to client_id and rename it honestly, or persist the S11 entity/evidence model with separate client/entity keys and relationships.

findings.title: The learner reaches the SQL gate without a theory-local worked model for the full CRUD vocabulary or one of the three domain tables the para…
findings.evidence: Roadmap/outcome says schema, CRUD and joins and prose names clients, transactions and evidence. The theory DDL creates only clients/evidence and demonstrates CREATE/INSERT/SELECT; no transactions table and no UPDATE/DELETE path is shown.
findings.impact: The learner reaches the SQL gate without a theory-local worked model for the full CRUD vocabulary or one of the three domain tables the paragraph claims exists.
findings.fix: Either narrow the outcome to create/insert/select/join or add a minimal transactions table plus one UPDATE and clearly scoped DELETE/soft-delete example.

findings.title: The learner can mistake naming convention for enforced referential integrity and publish incomplete case joins without a database error.
findings.evidence: evidence.entity_id is only a TEXT column. No FOREIGN KEY is declared or enabled; the callout explicitly says 'FKs lógicas primero'. Orphan evidence is therefore accepted and an inner JOIN silently drops it.
findings.impact: The learner can mistake naming convention for enforced referential integrity and publish incomplete case joins without a database error.
findings.fix: Declare the actual foreign key for the chosen model, enable PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON per connection, and add an orphan-insert negative example; otherwise label the schema intentionally non-enforcing and reconcile orphans explicitly.

findings.title: The section's central privacy boundary remains a sentence; the learner has no executable guard preventing document_id/name/account fields fr…
findings.evidence: Prose promises an allowlist ALLOWED={'address','city','country'} and says allowed_for_public_geocoder returns False when document_id appears. No such function or egress-check code exists in the canonical theory block.
findings.impact: The section's central privacy boundary remains a sentence; the learner has no executable guard preventing document_id/name/account fields from being sent to a provider adapter.
findings.fix: Implement sanitize_geocoder_payload/allowed_for_public_geocoder before the geocoder call and demonstrate an allowed payload plus a blocked document_id payload.

findings.title: A reasonable learner can recognize labels yet not know whether they denote a capstone increment, case, policy level, queue, or data-boundary…
findings.evidence: CP-N1-C, CASO-LIM-012, N1, DLQ, egress and related internal/ops labels appear before one stable learner-facing expansion; DLQ appears in a figure alt without definition.
findings.impact: A reasonable learner can recognize labels yet not know whether they denote a capstone increment, case, policy level, queue, or data-boundary concept.
findings.fix: Expand CP-N1-C and CASO-LIM-012 once, define N1 as the course-local retry policy, spell out dead-letter queue before DLQ, and keep egress paired with the Spanish meaning salida de datos.

findings.title: The visual summary teaches a broader retry policy than the text and can override the narrower rule the learner is supposed to implement.
findings.evidence: Figure alt says '5xx reintenta acotado, 4xx de negocio va a DLQ' while the local N1 prose says only 429/503/timeouts retry and explicitly maps 500 to fail_server without blind retry.
findings.impact: The visual summary teaches a broader retry policy than the text and can override the narrower rule the learner is supposed to implement.
findings.fix: Make the figure use the exact course table: timeout/429/503 -> bounded retry; 400 -> fix request; 404 -> missing; 500 -> fail_server under N1.

findings.title: The only indexing example teaches that indexes are added by ritual rather than because a query plan needs them, while omitting the child/joi…
findings.evidence: document_id is declared UNIQUE and then CREATE INDEX idx_doc ON clients(document_id) creates another index over the same column; the prose also mentions entity_id indexing but no entity_id index is demonstrated.
findings.impact: The only indexing example teaches that indexes are added by ritual rather than because a query plan needs them, while omitting the child/join key that would be a more defensible candidate.
findings.fix: Remove the redundant document_id index, add an entity/join-key index only if the schema/query requires it, and show EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN or at least the query that motivates the index.

findings.title: A malformed provider payload can crash the pipeline at the validation function rather than enter the documented invalid-coordinate path.
findings.evidence: Prose explicitly says strings are invalid coordinates and should be rejected. valid_coord('bad', -77) raises TypeError instead of returning False or an explicit domain error; 91 and NaN happen to produce False.
findings.impact: A malformed provider payload can crash the pipeline at the validation function rather than enter the documented invalid-coordinate path.
findings.fix: Validate numeric type/finite value first and return a documented result or raise one deliberate validation error.

findings.title: The learner can describe the result as a WGS84 geodesic or route distance rather than a spherical straight-line surface approximation from l…
findings.evidence: Text says Haversine estimates km 'entre dos puntos WGS84 con radio R=6371 km'. The implemented formula is a spherical Haversine approximation using a mean radius; WGS84 itself is an ellipsoid.
findings.impact: The learner can describe the result as a WGS84 geodesic or route distance rather than a spherical straight-line surface approximation from lat/lon coordinates.
findings.fix: Say 'para coordenadas lat/lon expresadas en WGS84, usamos aquí una aproximación esférica Haversine con R=6371 km; no es distancia de ruta ni geodésica elipsoidal exacta'.

findings.title: The learner can record a plausible-looking timestamp unrelated to the actual acquisition event and call the manifest provenance.
findings.evidence: The code imports time and computes cache age using the actual clock, but fetched_at is hard-coded to 2026-07-20T12:00:00Z while prose describes it as metadata of each fetch.
findings.impact: The learner can record a plausible-looking timestamp unrelated to the actual acquisition event and call the manifest provenance.
findings.fix: Inject a clock for deterministic tests and set fetched_at from that clock at the actual fetch/cache decision boundary.

findings.title: An auditor sees that fallback happened but cannot determine why or which frozen source supplied the coordinates.
findings.evidence: Callout says fallback leaves mode=offline and the reason in provenance. The returned dict contains mode only; there is no provenance object, failure reason, source version or offline dataset identity.
findings.impact: An auditor sees that fallback happened but cannot determine why or which frozen source supplied the coordinates.
findings.fix: Return/record fallback_reason, source_id/version, generated_at and mode alongside the value.

findings.title: A beginner reasonably expects PRIMARY KEY to guarantee a non-null identity and may persist rows with no ID while believing the constraint bl…
findings.evidence: Schema uses id TEXT PRIMARY KEY without NOT NULL. In ordinary SQLite rowid tables this historical quirk can permit NULL primary-key values; an execution check inserted (NULL,'x') successfully.
findings.impact: A beginner reasonably expects PRIMARY KEY to guarantee a non-null identity and may persist rows with no ID while believing the constraint blocks them.
findings.fix: Declare TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL (or an appropriate STRICT/WITHOUT ROWID design) and demonstrate the negative insert if identity presence matters.

findings.title: The learner can cache geocoder results indefinitely or without normalized keys/provider terms because no domain-specific cache contract is s…
findings.evidence: Outcome/prose requires caching geocodes under provider TTL/policy. T4-B has no cache code or provider-policy artifact; it only points back to the generic URL cache from T2-A, which itself has auth-scope issues.
findings.impact: The learner can cache geocoder results indefinitely or without normalized keys/provider terms because no domain-specific cache contract is shown.
findings.fix: Add a tiny geocode cache keyed by normalized authorized query + provider/version with explicit TTL/policy and no sensitive raw address when policy forbids storage.

findings.title: The learner can think response.json() and JSON decoding failure are independent mechanisms rather than two views of the same response body.
findings.evidence: MockResponse.json() simply returns the prebuilt _payload and never parses self.text. parse_json_body separately parses raw text. The same response object therefore does not model the causal path response bytes/text -> JSON decode -> payload/error.
findings.impact: The learner can think response.json() and JSON decoding failure are independent mechanisms rather than two views of the same response body.
findings.fix: Make the mock response store text and let json() call json.loads(text), so invalid body raises the same decode error the adapter must classify.

findings.title: The capstone can treat missing or unsafe infrastructure as a solved prerequisite and wire it into the final product without ever seeing a co…
findings.evidence: S13 says the S12 HTTP client with timeout/retries and geographic egress policy are inherited and will not be rebuilt. The effective S12 ledger leaves real HTTP request construction MENTION_ONLY, retry/backoff MISCONCEPTION_RISK and egress enforcement PARTIAL/prose-only.
findings.impact: The capstone can treat missing or unsafe infrastructure as a solved prerequisite and wire it into the final product without ever seeing a correct implementation.
findings.fix: Revalidate only the unsafe S12 edges at S13 entry: one real/faked synchronous GET adapter, bounded idempotent retry, and executable egress guard before integration.

findings.title: The learner can implement a key formatter but cannot implement blocking as a candidate-generation algorithm; true pairs separated by the onl…
findings.evidence: Prose says blocking uses several keys and a document key rescues pairs split by the surname/region key. The code has one block_key and scores an already-selected pair; it never generates candidate pairs or unions multiple blocking passes.
findings.impact: The learner can implement a key formatter but cannot implement blocking as a candidate-generation algorithm; true pairs separated by the only key are never compared.
findings.fix: Show a tiny candidate generator that produces pairs from at least two blocking keys and unions/deduplicates the candidate pairs before fine comparison.

findings.title: A learner cannot know which contract is canonical and will produce different scores depending on whether they copied prose or code.
findings.evidence: The paragraph defines 1.0 for same document+block, 0.5 for same document only, and 0.0 otherwise. Canonical theory code implements only 1.0 when both match, else 0.0. Spot-check same document/different region returned 0.0.
findings.impact: A learner cannot know which contract is canonical and will produce different scores depending on whether they copied prose or code.
findings.fix: Make the theory code implement exactly the documented 1.0/0.5/0.0 cascade and test all three branches.

findings.title: Bad input crashes the capstone instead of producing a reviewable invalid-data state, contradicting the safety model being taught.
findings.evidence: Prose says missing document, empty name or unusable block fails closed. block_key indexes parts[0] on an empty name and calls casefold on region without validation. Spot-checks raised IndexError for empty name and AttributeError for region=None.
findings.impact: Bad input crashes the capstone instead of producing a reviewable invalid-data state, contradicting the safety model being taught.
findings.fix: Validate required strings before normalization/blocking and return an explicit invalid_candidate/error result rather than indexing/casefolding unchecked values.

findings.title: The learner is taught to knowingly encode a parsing rule that breaks common multi-token given names, causing systematic missed candidates wh…
findings.evidence: The lesson explicitly demonstrates that parts[1] misclassifies its own opening example 'Ana María Quispe Rojas' as surname 'maría', yet makes parts[1] the canonical paternal-surname rule. Prior S07 name parsing remains MISCONCEPTION_RISK.
findings.impact: The learner is taught to knowingly encode a parsing rule that breaks common multi-token given names, causing systematic missed candidates when document evidence is absent or dirty.
findings.fix: Use the already-structured apellido_paterno field in the synthetic schema; if only a full name is available, label token parsing as a lossy fallback and route ambiguity to review instead of making it canonical.

findings.title: The learner can accept poor candidate recall believing human review repairs missed pairs that humans never see.
findings.evidence: The text says imperfect recall is compensated by the clerical queue. A queue only reviews candidates routed to it; false negatives rejected below the queue or eliminated during blocking are never recovered by that queue.
findings.impact: The learner can accept poor candidate recall believing human review repairs missed pairs that humans never see.
findings.fix: State that clerical review reduces risk only for surfaced uncertain candidates; blocking/candidate recall must be measured separately because missed candidates are unrecoverable downstream.

findings.title: Corrupt evaluation data can silently look like zero errors instead of invalid evaluation evidence.
findings.evidence: Prose says non-finite label/score input fails closed. pr_metrics accepts arbitrary tuple values and silently ignores malformed labels/predictions. Spot-check malformed values produced tp=fp=fn=0 rather than an error.
findings.impact: Corrupt evaluation data can silently look like zero errors instead of invalid evaluation evidence.
findings.fix: Validate truth/prediction values against an explicit binary schema before counting; reject malformed/nonfinite inputs with a clear error.

findings.title: The learner believes a surname-similarity feature is being computed while the implementation also penalizes unrelated given-name tokens, cor…
findings.evidence: The signal is named surname_jaccard, but surname_overlap tokenizes each full name. For 'Ana Quispe Rojas' vs 'Luis Quispe Díaz' the code reports 0.2 because given names are in the union; the surnames alone have Jaccard 1/3 ≈ 0.333.
findings.impact: The learner believes a surname-similarity feature is being computed while the implementation also penalizes unrelated given-name tokens, corrupting the meaning of the feature and its weight.
findings.fix: Compute Jaccard from explicit surname fields/tokens only, or rename the feature to full_name_token_jaccard and change the prose/weights accordingly.

findings.title: Exactly the missing-field case that prose says should fail closed can crash score calculation instead of producing an explicit unavailable s…
findings.evidence: shared_contact returns None when a field is missing and '' when empty because it uses 'a.get(field) and ...'. The weighted formula expects a numeric/boolean; 0.5 * None raises TypeError.
findings.impact: Exactly the missing-field case that prose says should fail closed can crash score calculation instead of producing an explicit unavailable signal.
findings.fix: Return an explicit signal state/value such as False plus available=False, and make scoring policy handle unavailable evidence deliberately.

findings.title: The learner can persist/reuse one 'km' on an entity as if it were universally meaningful, producing impossible relationship evidence when th…
findings.evidence: Each entity dict carries a single km field and geo_close_pair requires both entities to report the same km. Distance is a property of a pair of coordinates/entities, not an intrinsic per-entity attribute; one entity has different distances to different peers.
findings.impact: The learner can persist/reuse one 'km' on an entity as if it were universally meaningful, producing impossible relationship evidence when the entity is compared with multiple peers.
findings.fix: Compute or store distance on the pair/evidence object from two coordinates, with source/provenance, never as a scalar property of each entity.

findings.title: Direction-sensitive transaction evidence is silently converted into undirected adjacency, so the dashboard can describe a common payee patte…
findings.evidence: Prose defines common counterparties as 'A and C pay D'. counterparties treats edges as undirected. Counterexample A->D and D->C still yields D as common even though C did not pay D.
findings.impact: Direction-sensitive transaction evidence is silently converted into undirected adjacency, so the dashboard can describe a common payee pattern that did not occur.
findings.fix: Define the intended relation (e.g. outgoing payees) and intersect outgoing_counterparties(A) with outgoing_counterparties(C); teach a separate undirected relation only if desired and name it differently.

findings.title: The learner is taught that disagreement between deliberately independent scores is evidence of uncertainty, reintroducing the conceptual fus…
findings.evidence: The lesson insists ER and relationship are different constructs, then sets uncertainty=high whenever |ER-REL|>0.5. High ER and low REL can be completely coherent: the same person/identity can have little relationship evidence to another entity.
findings.impact: The learner is taught that disagreement between deliberately independent scores is evidence of uncertainty, reintroducing the conceptual fusion the lesson repeatedly warns against.
findings.fix: Compute uncertainty from evidence quality within each construct (missing fields, contradictory identity rules, provenance/quality) rather than from numerical distance between ER and REL.

findings.title: A reviewer can recompute the 0.6/0.4 blend but cannot reconstruct why ER or REL had their values, so the underlying decision remains unaudit…
findings.evidence: The lesson requires a reviewer to reconstruct the decision in five minutes and says each score must show the signals that produced it. explain() exposes only aggregate ER, aggregate REL, missing fields and rules_version; it omits component rules/signals, weights, pair/case identity, source/provenance and calculation inputs.
findings.impact: A reviewer can recompute the 0.6/0.4 blend but cannot reconstruct why ER or REL had their values, so the underlying decision remains unauditable.
findings.fix: Include component evidence with raw/normalized synthetic inputs or stable references, weights/rules fired, pair/case id, source/provenance and rules version.

findings.title: The learner can naturally pass the just-created evidence_score into the next subsection and accept an identity pair because relationship evi…
findings.evidence: T3-A correctly warns that evidence_score must never drive identity acceptance, but the immediately following function is decide_ops_status(score, uncertainty) and its prose/table use the generic term score rather than entity_resolution_score.
findings.impact: The learner can naturally pass the just-created evidence_score into the next subsection and accept an identity pair because relationship evidence pushed the blended score over 0.8.
findings.fix: Rename the parameter/table column to entity_resolution_score and show the exact call site from a case card, keeping evidence_score only for queue ordering.

findings.title: A Windows learner can be blocked from performing a mandatory safety audit by tooling the course never established portably.
findings.evidence: A gate-level portfolio audit instructs the learner to use grep. S01 did not leave shell portability safe to inherit; grep is not a guaranteed default command on Windows.
findings.impact: A Windows learner can be blocked from performing a mandatory safety audit by tooling the course never established portably.
findings.fix: Provide a Python stdlib repository scan as the canonical cross-platform mechanism; optionally mention grep as a Unix convenience.

findings.title: The most important decision policy loses row/column structure in the rendered lesson, raising comparison load and making exact boundary rule…
findings.evidence: The decision table is authored as twelve separate paragraph strings containing Markdown table rows. SectionView joins theory paragraphs with blank lines. RichText.parseBlocks supports paragraphs/lists/code/callouts but no table parsing; therefore the central matrix is parsed as literal pipe-delimited paragraphs, not a table.
findings.impact: The most important decision policy loses row/column structure in the rendered lesson, raising comparison load and making exact boundary rules harder to scan or access semantically.
findings.fix: Represent the matrix with a renderer-supported structure (ordered list or dedicated table component) or add tested Markdown-table support to RichText.

findings.title: A learner can finish all S13 theory code yet still have no learner-visible path from those dictionaries to the dashboard/map artifact that t…
findings.evidence: The theory promises an auditable dashboard/map scaffold but dashboard_scaffold.py only builds three dictionaries and prints rows; it creates no HTML/UI/map. A standalone FamiliarityDashboard component exists in the app, but the S13 lesson neither embeds nor links to that #familiarity view, and the normal SectionView does not mount it.
findings.impact: A learner can finish all S13 theory code yet still have no learner-visible path from those dictionaries to the dashboard/map artifact that the outcome and gate require.
findings.fix: Provide/teach a minimal static scaffold artifact in the lesson or explicitly link/embed the supplied dashboard template and show how the S13 case schema feeds it.

findings.title: A learner can satisfy S13's stated CF-1 and be told the level closes while missing mandatory artifacts required by the curriculum authority.
findings.evidence: S13 repeatedly defines CF-1 as privacy sheet + demo + runbook/access. The authoritative roadmap defines CF-1 as stakeholders, jobs-to-be-done, success metrics, constraints/no-go, contracts and base demo, with owner/reviewer and complete traceability; checkpoint records version/revision, date, paths/hashes, commands, results and issues.
findings.impact: A learner can satisfy S13's stated CF-1 and be told the level closes while missing mandatory artifacts required by the curriculum authority.
findings.fix: Replace S13's local CF-1 checklist with the authoritative CF-1 schema and show one complete synthetic manifest row.

findings.title: The learner can self-attest thirteen text lines instead of executing the regression evidence required for promotion.
findings.evidence: S13 reduces level regression to re-running 'critical checks' from LEVEL1_REGRESSION_MATRIX and noting pass/fail; ops_cf1.py only prints 'S01-S13 checklist required'. Roadmap requires critical tests of all three capstones, E2E integration, a recovery item per previous topic and privacy/security controls with explicit gate evidence.
findings.impact: The learner can self-attest thirteen text lines instead of executing the regression evidence required for promotion.
findings.fix: Teach an executable regression manifest/harness that records command, exit/result, evidence path/hash and criticality for each required capstone/E2E/privacy/security check.

findings.title: The learner is instructed to demonstrate a command whose module is neither built nor supplied by the theory, so the promised reproducible ga…
findings.evidence: The lesson requires one-command clean-machine reproduction with 'python -m demo_n1_dashboard --synthetic', but theory only prints that string and repository code search did not find a demo_n1_dashboard module on main.
findings.impact: The learner is instructed to demonstrate a command whose module is neither built nor supplied by the theory, so the promised reproducible gate can fail immediately with module-not-found.
findings.fix: Provide the module/template as an explicit learner artifact or teach how to create it from the completed pipeline, then run the exact command as verification instead of printing it.

findings.title: A learner can follow the local sentence yet not know whether a label names a metric, project checkpoint, course-internal gate, interface art…
findings.evidence: ER, CP-N1-C, CF-1, gate, scaffold, runbook, egress and cola clerical recur as compact labels; several are expanded only after they already carry instructional weight.
findings.impact: A learner can follow the local sentence yet not know whether a label names a metric, project checkpoint, course-internal gate, interface artifact or operational procedure.
findings.fix: Use Spanish head terms first and expand each internal acronym/ID once at first use; keep the short label only afterward.

findings.title: Scores in [0.7,0.8) have two incompatible operational policies depending on which subsection the learner follows.
findings.evidence: T1-B defines the clerical band as [0.4, 0.7], while T3-B routes every score from 0.4 up to but not including 0.8 to needs_review.
findings.impact: Scores in [0.7,0.8) have two incompatible operational policies depending on which subsection the learner follows.
findings.fix: Choose one review band and reuse the same named thresholds everywhere.

findings.title: A reviewer can interpret lack of evaluable positives as genuine model performance of 0.0 and miss that the evaluation set/prediction policy…
findings.evidence: When TP+FP or TP+FN is zero, the helper returns 0.0 without distinguishing 'metric is undefined because denominator is zero' from a measured precision/recall of zero.
findings.impact: A reviewer can interpret lack of evaluable positives as genuine model performance of 0.0 and miss that the evaluation set/prediction policy is degenerate.
findings.fix: Return/print an explicit undefined marker or status alongside the metric when the denominator is zero.

findings.title: The learner reaches the capstone without a canonical treatment of two roadmap-required relationship signals or their missing/normalization s…
findings.evidence: Roadmap T2 calls for shared email/phone/address plus distance/surnames. Theory's canonical relationship implementation demonstrates phone, geo and name-token overlap only; email/address are not integrated into the taught score/evidence model.
findings.impact: The learner reaches the capstone without a canonical treatment of two roadmap-required relationship signals or their missing/normalization semantics.
findings.fix: Add one compact signal registry/example that includes email and address availability/normalization, even if their N1 weight is zero or they remain explanatory evidence.

findings.title: The learner can transfer the synthetic-display technique to real cases and interpret masked names as anonymized/safe-to-share data.
findings.evidence: The synthetic demo replaces every name token with first initial + *** and calls this pseudonymization, but it does not state that initials combined with city/map/other quasi-identifiers may remain linkable in real data.
findings.impact: The learner can transfer the synthetic-display technique to real cases and interpret masked names as anonymized/safe-to-share data.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: display masking/pseudonymization reduces direct exposure but does not anonymize real records; real-data release requires separate privacy assessment/minimization.

findings.title: A learner can present a few labels as a privacy control without specifying retention or what each role may actually see/do.
findings.evidence: Prose says the sheet fixes local retention, viewer/reviewer access and what leaves the environment. Code records data_class, pii_real, egress label and role names, but no retention period/rule, no permission matrix and no evidence behind the self-assertion pii_real=False.
findings.impact: A learner can present a few labels as a privacy control without specifying retention or what each role may actually see/do.
findings.fix: Add retention, field-level/operation-level access notes, egress fields and evidence/source showing the fixture is synthetic.

findings.title: The learner can apply a rote three-word response without identifying what leaked, where it propagated, whether credentials remain active, or…
findings.evidence: The same trigger 'token_or_name_in_log' always produces rotate_secret, redact_logs, postmortem. Secret exposure and personal-data exposure have different first containment/evidence/notification questions; rotating a secret does not remediate a leaked name.
findings.impact: The learner can apply a rote three-word response without identifying what leaked, where it propagated, whether credentials remain active, or what privacy containment is needed.
findings.fix: Split secret_leak and pii_log_leak branches with causal actions; define postmortem in plain language and record affected logs/scope before claiming closure.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede formar la regla falsa 'mezclar tipos hace que ndarray deje de ser homogéneo o NumPy vuelva…
findings.evidence: La analogía dice que si mezclas textos y números 'se pierde la ventaja y vuelves a contar monedas'. NumPy intenta encontrar un dtype común: por ejemplo int+float puede convertirse a float y seguir operando vectorizadamente; int+texto puede convertirse a Unicode; mezclas con None pueden terminar en object y perder muchas ventajas numéricas.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede formar la regla falsa 'mezclar tipos hace que ndarray deje de ser homogéneo o NumPy vuelva automáticamente a un loop Python'.
findings.fix: Explicar coerción a dtype común y distinguir dtype numérico común de string/object, donde operaciones numéricas pueden cambiar o dejar de estar disponibles.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede confiar en que una operación sin ValueError tiene la alineación de negocio correcta y publ…
findings.evidence: La apertura afirma que 'casi todo error de NumPy es un desacuerdo entre formas' y que 'ese desacuerdo se detecta al instante'. T2-B reconoce después que shapes compatibles pueden broadcastar de forma semánticamente equivocada. NumPy solo valida compatibilidad sintáctica de broadcasting, no la intención del eje.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede confiar en que una operación sin ValueError tiene la alineación de negocio correcta y publicar una métrica calculada contra el eje equivocado.
findings.fix: Reformular: muchos errores son de forma; incompatibilidad puede fallar ruidosamente, pero una compatibilidad válida también puede ser semánticamente incorrecta, por lo que hay que validar significado y shape esperado.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede implementar validación de inputs con assert después de que la misma lección explicó por qu…
findings.evidence: T1-A dice explícitamente 'No uses assert para esto' al validar input externo porque -O elimina asserts. El callout inmediatamente permite documentar dtype/shape '(o asertarlos)' y T2-B vuelve a ordenar 'aserta la compatibilidad' si el batch cambia.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede implementar validación de inputs con assert después de que la misma lección explicó por qué esa validación desaparece con python -O.
findings.fix: Reservar assert para invariantes internas; usar if + ValueError/TypeError para contratos de entrada en callout y T2-B.
findings.location: S14-T1-A p2 + T1-A callout + S14-T2-B p3

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede escribir el manejo/test para la excepción equivocada y no entender por qué el caso real no…
findings.evidence: El párrafo dice correctamente que una máscara desalineada lanza IndexError; el callout dice 'de lo contrario ValueError'. NumPy documenta IndexError para shape booleano que no coincide con las dimensiones indexadas.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede escribir el manejo/test para la excepción equivocada y no entender por qué el caso real no entra en except ValueError.
findings.fix: Cambiar ValueError por IndexError en el callout y conservar un ejemplo mínimo que lo demuestre.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede clasificar automáticamente cualquier NaN como dato ausente y ocultar un error de cálculo que debía i…
findings.evidence: La oración absoluta 'un NaN no es cero: es ausencia de medición' convierte una convención del fixture en semántica universal. NaN también puede surgir de operaciones inválidas o emplearse como sentinel; su significado depende del contrato de datos.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede clasificar automáticamente cualquier NaN como dato ausente y ocultar un error de cálculo que debía investigarse.
findings.fix: Decir: 'En este fixture usamos NaN para representar ausencia de medición; en otro pipeline debes verificar por qué apareció antes de decidir si omitirlo, rechazarlo o tratarlo como error.'

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede escoger rtol/atol como múltiplos arbitrarios de eps y declarar equivalentes resultados que incumplen…
findings.evidence: El texto define correctamente finfo(float).eps como separación alrededor de 1.0, pero añade que esa escala 'es lo que necesitas para elegir la tolerancia de un allclose'. eps no determina por sí solo el error aceptable de un algoritmo ni la tolerancia de negocio; el espaciado cambia con la magnitud y el error acumulado depende de operaciones/condicionamiento.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede escoger rtol/atol como múltiplos arbitrarios de eps y declarar equivalentes resultados que incumplen la precisión requerida o rechazar resultados correctos a otra escala.
findings.fix: Separar machine epsilon de error budget: eps ilustra resolución cerca de 1; rtol/atol se justifican con escala, algoritmo y tolerancia del dominio.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede ejecutar código correcto, obtener False y creer que falló; o puede publicar un único ratio favorable…
findings.evidence: La lección llama 'benchmark honesto' a una sola medición loop y una sola np.dot y fija output ratio_gt_1 True. Spot-check del mismo patrón mostró una primera corrida ~0.97 y corridas posteriores muy superiores a 1 por warm-up/ruido. La documentación de timeit recomienda repetir mediciones porque otros procesos y overhead afectan tiempos cortos.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede ejecutar código correcto, obtener False y creer que falló; o puede publicar un único ratio favorable como evidencia estable de rendimiento.
findings.fix: Hacer warm-up y varias repeticiones con timeit/perf_counter, reportar vector/resumen de tiempos y no convertir speedup>1 en output determinista ni criterio de corrección.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede creer que ha implementado un guard de memoria cuando en realidad comprueba el presupuesto después de…
findings.evidence: El presupuesto se expresa como pair.nbytes <= max_bytes, que solo puede consultarse después de materializar la matriz n×n. Con n grande, la asignación puede agotar RAM antes de que exista pair para comprobar nbytes.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede creer que ha implementado un guard de memoria cuando en realidad comprueba el presupuesto después del posible OOM.
findings.fix: Calcular required_bytes = n*n*np.dtype(dtype).itemsize antes de construir pair; solo materializar si required_bytes <= max_bytes.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, una implementación vectorizada puede devolver una forma equivocada y aun pasar el test de equivalencia numérica.
findings.evidence: La sección trata shape como parte del contrato pero propone allclose como oráculo de equivalencia sin exigir shape igual. NumPy allclose aplica broadcasting, por lo que arrays de shapes diferentes pueden devolver True si sus valores broadcastados son cercanos.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, una implementación vectorizada puede devolver una forma equivocada y aun pasar el test de equivalencia numérica.
findings.fix: Primero exigir a.shape == b.shape (y shape esperado); después aplicar assert_allclose a los valores.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, dos implementaciones semánticamente equivalentes respecto a faltantes pueden fallar, o un alumno puede activar equal…
findings.evidence: T3-B admite NaN/inf como edge cases, pero T4-B no define cómo entran al contrato de equivalencia. allclose considera NaN distinto por defecto salvo equal_nan=True y trata inf por posición/signo. Usar equal_nan=True sin política también puede ocultar errores.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, dos implementaciones semánticamente equivalentes respecto a faltantes pueden fallar, o un alumno puede activar equal_nan=True indiscriminadamente y declarar equivalentes NaNs que nacieron de causas distintas.
findings.fix: Comparar primero máscaras de no-finitos según política; luego comparar valores finitos. Usar equal_nan=True solo si el contrato declara que NaN en la misma posición representa el mismo estado.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede creer que convertir una métrica a NumPy la vuelve auditable aunque no conserve definición,…
findings.evidence: La relevancia laboral cierra con 'Es la base para cualquier métrica de calidad de datos que un comité pueda auditar', atribuyendo auditabilidad al cómputo vectorizado. Vectorizar acelera/estructura cálculo numérico; la auditabilidad depende además de contrato, procedencia, versión, pruebas y explicación.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede creer que convertir una métrica a NumPy la vuelve auditable aunque no conserve definición, fuente, política de faltantes ni evidencia de validación.
findings.fix: Reemplazar la causalidad por: NumPy hace eficientes las métricas; contratos, provenance y tests hacen auditable su significado.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un principiante puede memorizar una lista de atributos sin poder dibujar qué representa shape=(4,), distinguir dimen…
findings.evidence: El primer párrafo técnico introduce en una sola unidad ndarray, contiguous/strided, homogeneous, compiled ufunc, dtype, shape, ndim, itemsize y CP-N2-A antes de un worked representation de una dimensión y dos dimensiones.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un principiante puede memorizar una lista de atributos sin poder dibujar qué representa shape=(4,), distinguir dimensión de tamaño o explicar para qué sirve cada atributo.
findings.fix: Dividir el párrafo en representación concreta array→dtype→shape y relegar strided/itemsize/CP-N2-A a una segunda oración o referencia.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede creer que dtype=int garantiza resultados enteros al dividir o que object significa literalmente 'Num…
findings.evidence: El texto dice que dtype explícito evita sorpresas 'int vs float en divisiones' y presenta object como 'lento y no vectorizable'. La división verdadera de arrays enteros puede producir float, y object arrays pueden ejecutar algunas ufuncs/operaciones aunque frecuentemente deleguen en objetos Python y pierdan eficiencia/garantías numéricas.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede creer que dtype=int garantiza resultados enteros al dividir o que object significa literalmente 'NumPy no puede vectorizar ninguna operación'.
findings.fix: Decir que dtype hace visible el contrato de almacenamiento y coerción, pero cada operación tiene reglas de promoción; object suele perder ventajas y seguridad numérica, no es una prohibición absoluta.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede tratar copy/view como comportamiento incierto y añadir copias defensivas innecesarias o, al revés, a…
findings.evidence: La lección dice que fancy indexing y máscaras 'suelen' copiar. La regla pedagógica útil y documentada por NumPy es más fuerte: advanced indexing (entero o booleano) devuelve copia; basic slicing devuelve view.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede tratar copy/view como comportamiento incierto y añadir copias defensivas innecesarias o, al revés, asumir sharing donde advanced indexing ya aisló los datos.
findings.fix: Enseñar primero la regla determinista basic slicing→view / advanced indexing→copy; dejar excepciones/operaciones que producen views por otras vías fuera del modelo inicial.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede validar dtype y shape, recibir valores semánticamente inválidos y publicar una tasa imposible >1 cre…
findings.evidence: Completitud se calcula con mean(flags) y el texto define flags como presencia 1/0, pero no enseña a validar el dominio binario. Un array [1,2] produce una 'completitud' 1.5 sin error de dtype/shape.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede validar dtype y shape, recibir valores semánticamente inválidos y publicar una tasa imposible >1 creyendo que el contrato del ndarray bastaba.
findings.fix: Añadir un invariante simple antes de la reducción: valores permitidos {0,1} o bool; entrada fuera del dominio → ValueError.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede sufrir ZeroDivisionError en un lote vacío o inventar un valor que altera el significado de la métric…
findings.evidence: La fórmula de unicidad np.unique(ids).size / ids.size no define el caso ids.size==0; el cálculo divide por cero. Una métrica de data quality necesita distinguir lote vacío de unicidad 0 o 1.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede sufrir ZeroDivisionError en un lote vacío o inventar un valor que altera el significado de la métrica.
findings.fix: Definir política explícita para lote vacío (por ejemplo, devolver None/estado empty_batch o rechazarlo antes de calcular).

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede reconocer un ValueError de broadcasting pero no detectar el caso más peligroso señalado por la propi…
findings.evidence: El texto advierte que una alineación silenciosa puede ser peor que ValueError, pero el único worked code muestra un broadcast correcto y otro incompatible que falla. No muestra dos shapes técnicamente compatibles que correspondan a ejes distintos y produzcan un resultado válido pero equivocado.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede reconocer un ValueError de broadcasting pero no detectar el caso más peligroso señalado por la propia lección: el cálculo que corre y está mal alineado.
findings.fix: Añadir un microejemplo (2,3)+(3,) frente a (2,3)+(2,1), ambos válidos pero con semántica columna vs fila distinta, y exigir shape esperado por contrato.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede confundir dos mecanismos diferentes y buscar una llamada reshape inexistente para explicar una trans…
findings.evidence: El código usa np.array([0.5])[:, None] y comenta '(1,1) vía reshape'. `None`/newaxis inserta un eje mediante indexación; no se llamó reshape. El mismo subtema está enseñando newaxis como mecanismo nuevo.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede confundir dos mecanismos diferentes y buscar una llamada reshape inexistente para explicar una transformación hecha por newaxis.
findings.fix: Cambiar el comentario a '(1,1) insertando un eje con None/newaxis'.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un lote completamente inválido puede convertirse silenciosamente en una métrica nan y continuar por el pipeline sin…
findings.evidence: La receta finite=x[np.isfinite(x)]; mean(finite) no define qué ocurre si no queda ningún valor finito. NumPy devuelve nan con warning para una media vacía en vez de producir el rechazo explícito que la prosa fail-closed sugiere.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un lote completamente inválido puede convertirse silenciosamente en una métrica nan y continuar por el pipeline sin un estado de error distinguible.
findings.fix: Antes de mean, si finite.size==0 devolver/rechazar con estado no_valid_measurements y reportar tasa no-finita=1.0.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede copiar 1e-8 o 1e-6 como constantes rituales sin relacionarlas con escala, algoritmo o error permitid…
findings.evidence: La teoría dice elegir rtol/atol según la métrica, pero los ejemplos usan 1e-7/1e-9/1e-6 sin explicar de dónde salen. NumPy advierte que atol por defecto/elección puede ser inapropiado para valores pequeños y define la comparación respecto a una referencia.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno puede copiar 1e-8 o 1e-6 como constantes rituales sin relacionarlas con escala, algoritmo o error permitido por el negocio.
findings.fix: Añadir un ejemplo causal: definir primero el máximo error aceptable de la métrica y derivar/justificar atol/rtol para ese rango; mostrar un caso que pasa y uno que falla por ese umbral.

findings.title: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede seguir sintaxis local pero no saber qué compara el baseline, qué entrega CP-N2-A o qué sig…
findings.evidence: `baseline` aparece en el tagline antes de definirse al final de T4-B; `CP-N2-A` se usa como si el learner supiera qué artefacto nombra; `strided` aparece en la primera definición de ndarray sin microdefinición; `rebroadcast` aparece antes de una explicación causal completa.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede seguir sintaxis local pero no saber qué compara el baseline, qué entrega CP-N2-A o qué significa que un array sea strided, obligándolo a aportar conocimiento externo.
findings.fix: Definir baseline en primera aparición como versión de referencia; expandir CP-N2-A una vez; omitir strided del primer modelo o definirlo brevemente; usar 'volver a aplicar broadcasting' antes de rebroadcast.

findings.title: ¿La web actualmente desplegada sigue mostrando 18h para S14 mientras main declara estimatedHours=9?
findings.evidence: El snapshot público recuperable muestra 18h; main actual muestra 9. El snapshot web está cacheado/crawled, por lo que hace falta un render actual para convertirlo en finding.

findings.title: ¿Debe la plataforma bloquear S14 hasta reparar el gate N1 de S13?
findings.evidence: Roadmap declara prerequisite Nivel 1; S13 quedó REPAIR_REQUIRED. Esta auditoría lesson-only no infiere comportamiento de gating fuera de la lección.

findings.title: Shape/broadcast mental model: compatibility is conflated with correctness and the dangerous valid-but-wrong case is not worked.
Numerical evidence contract: eps, allclose, NaN and tolerances are individually named but not assembled into a safe equivalence policy.
Measurement-as-evidence: a one-shot benchmark and post-allocation memory check teach assertions about performance/resources after the point where evidence was needed.
Learner can expect row concat to reconcile duplicate business labels and silently build wrong reconciliation logic.
findings.evidence: Opening says Series concatenated by rows align by Index. pd.concat(axis=0) stacks along the index axis and can preserve duplicate labels; it does not reconcile labels like Series arithmetic.
findings.impact: Learner can expect row concat to reconcile duplicate business labels and silently build wrong reconciliation logic.
findings.fix: Separate Series arithmetic alignment, concat(axis=0) stacking and concat(axis=1) alignment.

findings.title: Learner can treat repeated client ids in a transaction table as invalid duplicate rows or lose the true transaction row identity.
findings.evidence: cliente_id is promoted as stable business Index while the gate covers transactions, where client ids legitimately repeat. pandas Index labels need not be unique.
findings.impact: Learner can treat repeated client ids in a transaction table as invalid duplicate rows or lose the true transaction row identity.
findings.fix: Use cliente_id as Index only for one-row-per-client data; transactions keep transaction_id or RangeIndex and cliente_id as a column.

findings.title: Learner can diagnose object dtype as proof of source corruption or assume every mixed-looking column must become object.
findings.evidence: Lesson says mixing a number and a name becomes object and seeing object in expected text means source mixed types. object can be explicitly requested or contain arbitrary Python objects; mixed CSV inference is parser/chunk dependent.
findings.impact: Learner can diagnose object dtype as proof of source corruption or assume every mixed-looking column must become object.
findings.fix: Teach object as a generic Python-object container; diagnose mixed inference from values/parser warnings and declared contract, not dtype alone.

findings.title: Printing a row count can be mistaken for reconciliation while missing/extra rows or columns pass.
findings.evidence: Gate requires row/column reconciliation; theory only prints len(df)=2 and never compares expected_rows or required_columns.
findings.impact: Printing a row count can be mistaken for reconciliation while missing/extra rows or columns pass.
findings.fix: Compare observed vs expected rows and required columns immediately after parsing, with explicit failure evidence.

findings.title: Learner on target version can look for a warning that no longer exists and infer the pattern is safe when it is absent.
findings.evidence: Target is pandas 3 but lesson repeatedly frames the issue as SettingWithCopy/SettingWithCopyWarning. pandas 3 removed that warning; chained assignment never updates parent under CoW and emits ChainedAssignmentError as a warning.
findings.impact: Learner on target version can look for a warning that no longer exists and infer the pattern is safe when it is absent.
findings.fix: Use pandas-3 CoW/ChainedAssignmentError terminology and one-step .loc assignment.

findings.title: Adding a schema entry changes nothing while learner believes schema drives behavior.
findings.evidence: schema dict is created but never iterated or used; conversions are hardcoded separately.
findings.impact: Adding a schema entry changes nothing while learner believes schema drives behavior.
findings.fix: Implement apply_schema that checks required columns and applies every schema entry, returning (df, report).

findings.title: Learner can claim Parquet competence without exercising engine dependency, Parquet bytes or round-trip type preservation.
findings.evidence: Roadmap requires CSV/Parquet/Excel, but theory never writes/reads Parquet and substitutes a dtype dict named parquet_contract.
findings.impact: Learner can claim Parquet competence without exercising engine dependency, Parquet bytes or round-trip type preservation.
findings.fix: Add a real optional Parquet round-trip with pyarrow/fastparquet; if unavailable, mark that gate not run rather than treating CSV+schema as equivalent.

findings.title: Reviewer cannot reconstruct what exact input bytes/config produced an output; different inputs/settings can share the same output provenance…
findings.evidence: Manifest source is only synthetic_clientes_v1 and content_sha256 hashes output CSV, not input source bytes or parser/schema configuration.
findings.impact: Reviewer cannot reconstruct what exact input bytes/config produced an output; different inputs/settings can share the same output provenance record.
findings.fix: Record input source/path, full input SHA-256, parser/schema version/options, coercion report, then output path/hash/shape separately.

findings.title: Learner can believe choosing Parquet automatically avoids reading unused columns/row groups regardless of read API/query plan.
findings.evidence: Projection pushdown is described as not something you activate, merely a consequence of layout; filter pruning is similarly presented. Layout enables skipping, but the reader/query engine must request columns/predicates and exploit metadata.
findings.impact: Learner can believe choosing Parquet automatically avoids reading unused columns/row groups regardless of read API/query plan.
findings.fix: Say Parquet enables pushdown; reader/engine must receive selected columns/filter and use metadata. Demonstrate with a real columns/filter read when engine exists.

findings.title: Learner can expect right.cliente_id column to be used by join(on='cliente_id') while pandas actually uses the right Index.
findings.evidence: Opening says merge and join(on=...) combine on named columns and Index does not participate. DataFrame.join(on=...) matches caller column(s) to the other object's Index; join defaults to index-on-index when on is omitted.
findings.impact: Learner can expect right.cliente_id column to be used by join(on='cliente_id') while pandas actually uses the right Index.
findings.fix: Teach merge(on=...) as column-oriented; teach DataFrame.join separately as index-oriented, including caller-column-to-other-index semantics.

findings.title: Learner can call a dtype map a complete schema and assume nullability, uniqueness/ranges/required columns are covered.
findings.evidence: Schema is defined as the set/map of dtypes while later claims assign it required-column and shape responsibilities.
findings.impact: Learner can call a dtype map a complete schema and assume nullability, uniqueness/ranges/required columns are covered.
findings.fix: Call it a minimum ingestion schema: required columns plus dtype/coercion policy; deeper constraints arrive in S16.

findings.title: Learner conflates API isolation with eager copying and transfers wrong memory/view reasoning from NumPy.
findings.evidence: CoW is glossed as 'escritura sobre copia automática', suggesting eager physical copying.
findings.impact: Learner conflates API isolation with eager copying and transfers wrong memory/view reasoning from NumPy.
findings.fix: Say derived objects behave independently at the API while pandas may share memory and defer physical copying until a write.

findings.title: Learner can universalize coercion+continue to critical identifiers/amounts that policy should reject or quarantine.
findings.evidence: errors='coerce' is called preferable to failing the batch if failures are counted.
findings.impact: Learner can universalize coercion+continue to critical identifiers/amounts that policy should reject or quarantine.
findings.fix: Frame coercion+report as a lab policy; critical fields may require rejection/quarantine under the data contract.

findings.title: Learner can rely on a short display fingerprint as a full artifact identifier.
findings.evidence: content_sha256 stores hexdigest()[:12], a 12-hex prefix, while field name implies complete SHA-256.
findings.impact: Learner can rely on a short display fingerprint as a full artifact identifier.
findings.fix: Store full digest as content_sha256 and optionally a separately named sha256_prefix.

findings.title: Learner imagines one whole-file block per column and misunderstands row-group IO/statistics.
findings.evidence: Lesson says Parquet stores first all client_id then all monto then all region. Actual hierarchy is file -> row groups -> one column chunk per column in each row group -> pages.
findings.impact: Learner imagines one whole-file block per column and misunderstands row-group IO/statistics.
findings.fix: Teach the actual file/row-group/column-chunk/page hierarchy first.

findings.title: Learner turns format comparison into a false absolute rule and misses parser-level projection.
findings.evidence: Text says row format forces all other 39 values to be read even if discarded. CSV reader must scan row text but usecols can avoid materializing unnecessary columns; exact work is parser-dependent.
findings.impact: Learner turns format comparison into a false absolute rule and misses parser-level projection.
findings.fix: Distinguish scanning row-oriented text from materializing/parsing selected columns.

findings.title: Learner misclassifies valid filtering as unsafe and fails to identify the actual mutation hazard.
findings.evidence: Lesson says boolean filters live inside loc. df[mask] is valid for read-only selection; the critical danger is chained assignment on writes.
findings.impact: Learner misclassifies valid filtering as unsafe and fails to identify the actual mutation hazard.
findings.fix: Prefer loc for explicit row+column selection/mutation but acknowledge df[mask] is valid read-only filtering.

findings.title: Learner can solve a row-group pruning problem by over-partitioning files and create a small-files problem.
findings.evidence: After row-group pruning, lesson moves directly to dataset partitioning and tiny-file tradeoffs, blending row groups inside files with file/directory partitions.
findings.impact: Learner can solve a row-group pruning problem by over-partitioning files and create a small-files problem.
