findings.fix: Separate dataset/file partitioning from row groups inside each Parquet file; both can aid pruning but have different controls/trade-offs.

findings.title: The lesson teaches isolated checks but never shows the causal pipeline raw input → rule results → disjoint clean/quarantine → metrics → pass/fail.
findings.evidence: The section promises a fail-closed quality suite, but each theory block operates on a fresh hand-built DataFrame. T4-B manually creates clean/quarantine tables instead of deriving them from the null, duplicate, normalization, schema and cross-field rules taught earlier.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can reproduce eight demos yet still be unable to build the integrated quality gate promised by the tagline and roadmap.
findings.fix: Add one compact theory example `run_quality_gate(raw, contract)` that reuses the taught checks and derives clean, quarantine, metrics and audit events from one input.
findings.location: tagline + opening p5 + reference p3 + T4-B
findings.prior_knowledge: S15 ingestion basics only; S16 itself must teach the quality-gate composition.

findings.title: Optionality answers whether null is allowed, not whether replacing it with a value is semantically valid.
findings.evidence: The opening distinguishes absent, not-applicable and real zero, but the executable policy reduces fields to required|optional. T1-B then allows median imputation for an optional field solely when its null rate is below a cap.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can infer `optional + null_rate <= cap => safe to impute` and invent values where null actually means not applicable or deliberately unknown.
findings.fix: Extend the field policy with an explicit null action/meaning such as required_fail, optional_keep_null or optional_impute(method=...), and state that the cap limits volume but does not authorize imputation.
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic missing-value identification; semantic missingness policy is new here.

findings.title: A next-section abstraction is used as the core implementation shortcut before it is taught.
findings.evidence: The conflict detector uses `groupby(...).transform('nunique')`, but the authoritative roadmap schedules groupby/agg/transform for S17. S16 gives syntax but no mental model of grouping, per-group aggregation or transform shape preservation.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can cargo-cult a groupby/transform expression without being able to predict which group a row belongs to or why the result aligns back to the original rows.
findings.fix: Use a small dict/set-based conflict detector with already learned constructs in S16, then teach groupby/transform from first principles in S17.
findings.prior_knowledge: Dictionaries/sets and pandas selection; groupby/transform is not yet creditable.

findings.title: The executable classifier is narrower/different from the contract it claims to demonstrate. Provenance columns such as batch/source would prevent otherwise business-identical rows from being classified as exact duplicates.
findings.evidence: The prose defines an exact duplicate by the relevant columns and says conflict checks should cover each attribute that must agree. The code calls `df.duplicated(keep=False)` with no subset, so every column is relevant, and checks only `region` for conflict.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can miss duplicate business records merely because provenance columns differ, or miss conflicts that occur in attributes other than region.
findings.fix: Declare `exact_cols` and `conflict_attrs` explicitly from the contract; use `duplicated(subset=exact_cols, keep=False)` and evaluate every conflict attribute with an explicit missing-value policy.
findings.prior_knowledge: pandas filtering and business-key concept.

findings.title: Input order is silently promoted into a business-resolution policy.
findings.evidence: For two C001 rows with scores 0.9 and 0.4 from sources a/b, the lesson resolves the key with `drop_duplicates(key, keep='first')`. No source-priority, timestamp, authoritative-system or review rule explains why input order should win.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can choose whichever conflicting row happened to arrive first and treat that arbitrary ordering as a defensible master-record resolution.
findings.fix: For unresolved conflicts, quarantine the whole key and exclude it from clean. Demonstrate promotion only after a deterministic documented rule such as authoritative-source priority or reviewed timestamp.
findings.prior_knowledge: Duplicate/conflict distinction taught immediately before.

findings.title: The two outputs called clean and quarantine are not mutually exclusive even though quarantine is later defined as rejected rows.
findings.evidence: `quarantine = df.loc[dup_mask]` contains both C001 rows, while `clean = df.drop_duplicates(key, keep='first')` also contains the first C001 row. For the three-row example, clean has 2 rows and quarantine has 2 rows: one source row is counted in both sets.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can report `rows_clean + rows_quarantine > rows_in`, double-count excluded data, and feed a quarantined row into S17.
findings.fix: Make outputs disjoint by default: unresolved duplicate-key groups go entirely to quarantine; only a row explicitly resolved/promoted leaves quarantine and enters clean, with an audit event.
findings.prior_knowledge: Set/disjointness intuition and row-count reconciliation from prior course goals.

findings.title: The normalizer is incompatible with the section's own null model.
findings.evidence: `stripped = df['region_raw'].str.strip()` can preserve missing values, but the following list comprehension calls `x.upper()` and `x.title()` unconditionally. `None`/`pd.NA` therefore raises instead of preserving or classifying the null.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can apply the canonical normalizer to an optional missing region and crash the batch instead of preserving null or routing it according to policy.
findings.fix: Use a null-safe `norm_region(x)` that returns `pd.NA` for missing inputs before applying `.upper()`/`.title()` to actual strings.
findings.prior_knowledge: T1-A has just established that nullable fields are normal and must follow policy.

findings.title: Invalid normalization outcomes are either silently converted to missing or crash outside the promised gate evidence model.
findings.evidence: `norm_money('abc')` becomes NaN through `or 'nan'` with no reason/count; malformed values such as repeated separators can raise ValueError; `parse_fecha` converts any unrecognized date to `pd.NaT`. The lesson preserves raw columns but emits no normalization-failure mask, code or quarantine evidence.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can transform bad source tokens into NaN/NaT without counting the failure and believe preserving `raw` alone satisfies «nunca arreglar en silencio».
findings.fix: After parsing, compute `raw.notna() & parsed.isna()` failure masks (or return value+reason) and attach structured reason codes/counts; catch deliberate parse failures at the quality boundary.
findings.prior_knowledge: T1-T2 quality evidence principle.

findings.title: The learner is asked to execute statistical formulas before the concepts that make them interpretable are taught.
findings.evidence: S16 uses median imputation and then introduces quantiles, IQR, the 1.5×IQR rule and mentions z-score, while the authoritative roadmap schedules center, dispersion and quantiles for S18. No local explanation establishes what a median/quantile/IQR represents or why 1.5 is a candidate heuristic.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can memorize `1.5 * IQR` as a universal truth detector or use median merely as a magic function without understanding the decision it encodes.
findings.fix: Give one bounded micro-model: median = middle value after ordering; Q1/Q3 split the lower/upper quarters; IQR=Q3-Q1; 1.5×IQR is a conventional candidate flag, not a business verdict. Defer z-score and deeper statistics to S18.
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic arithmetic; inferential/descriptive-statistics vocabulary is not yet creditable.

findings.title: S16 repeats the schema vocabulary but still does not make the declared contract dimensions executable.
findings.evidence: The prose defines schema contract as column presence, expected dtypes and field nullability. `contracts.py` checks only a set of expected column names; it never verifies dtype or nullable policy.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can pass the lesson's 'schema' gate with a required numeric column encoded as arbitrary strings or containing prohibited nulls.
findings.fix: Represent each required column with at least expected dtype + nullable flag and evaluate those properties before cross-field rules; report structured violations.
findings.prior_knowledge: S15 schema was already MISCONCEPTION_RISK and cannot be assumed executable.

findings.title: The supposed fail-closed guard is calculated but not used to gate downstream field access.
findings.evidence: The code computes `drift = expected - set(df.columns)` but immediately evaluates `df['fin'] < df['inicio']` and `df['monto'] < 0` before printing/returning the drift. If `fin` is missing, the example raises raw `KeyError('fin')`, exactly the outcome the prose says should be avoided.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can copy the canonical pattern, detect the missing column correctly, and still crash before producing the promised operator-facing diagnostic.
findings.fix: Check and report missing required columns first; if any exist, stop further field rules and return/emit a structured fail result before accessing those columns.
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic control flow and exceptions.

findings.title: The final report is a fabricated example rather than evidence generated by the gate.
findings.evidence: The prose promises null/duplicate/schema-failure rates in addition to row counts. The code manually constructs one-row clean and quarantine DataFrames and emits only rows_in, rows_clean, rows_quarantine and pass; none of the metrics are computed from the earlier checks.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can hard-code plausible metrics independently of the data-quality rules and still believe the quality suite is operational.
findings.fix: Derive all metrics from the same raw input and rule outputs, include per-rule counts/rates, and assert row conservation/disjointness where the policy partitions rows.
findings.prior_knowledge: Basic counts/rates; quality checks from this lesson.

findings.title: A critical operational behavior is asserted but never implemented at the process boundary.
findings.evidence: The prose promises `exit code != 0` together with JSON metrics when pass=False. The code only prints JSON and returns normally; the process therefore has no demonstrated non-zero status. The effective S10 ledger marks process exit status as MISCONCEPTION_RISK, so S16 cannot inherit this mechanism as mastered.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can equate printing `"pass": false` with making an orchestrator/OS observe failure, repeating an earlier course misconception.
findings.fix: Show a minimal `main() -> int` that emits metrics first and then exits non-zero on failed gate, e.g. `raise SystemExit(main())`; keep structured output available before exit.
findings.prior_knowledge: Process exit mapping is not creditable from S10.

findings.title: A learner can discard the earlier Decimal-for-money contract during cleaning and later aggregate approximate binary floats as canonical PEN.
findings.evidence: S16 calls normalized PEN outputs floats and norm_money returns float; S02 established Decimal for soles.
findings.impact: A learner can discard the earlier Decimal-for-money contract during cleaning and later aggregate approximate binary floats as canonical PEN.
findings.fix: Parse canonical PEN to Decimal. Teach any later Decimal-to-float analytics boundary explicitly.

findings.title: A learner can quarantine legitimate tail observations solely because IQR flagged them.
findings.evidence: The prose says stat outliers are flagged and quarantined, then says plausible 5000 must remain visible to S17; code marks 5000 stat-only, not domain_error.
findings.impact: A learner can quarantine legitimate tail observations solely because IQR flagged them.
findings.fix: Domain errors quarantine; stat-only plausible extremes stay clean with a flag unless a separate policy says otherwise.

findings.title: A storage sentinel is equated with one semantic cause.
findings.evidence: The text states `NaN` means «no sé». In pandas/NumPy-backed columns NaN can be used as a missing-value sentinel, but IEEE NaN means Not a Number and does not encode why a value is absent or invalid.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can treat every NaN as evidence that the source value was simply unknown, even when it arose from coercion or numeric computation.
findings.fix: Say: «En estas columnas pandas usa NaN como marca de valor faltante; NaN no explica por qué falta. Conserva además el motivo: ausente en origen, coerción fallida, etc.»
findings.prior_knowledge: S14 left NaN semantics unsafe; S16 must not collapse numeric NaN and business meaning.

findings.title: The output shape required to connect a rule failure to T4-B quarantine is missing.
findings.evidence: The prose says each rule returns a failure mask plus a readable error code for quarantine. The code only prints index lists under labels `cross_fail_idx` and `neg_idx`; it never constructs a quarantine reason field or rule-code record.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can identify row 1 as bad but still not know how to produce the promised row-level reason evidence when several rules fail.
findings.fix: Create a small violations table/list with row index/key, rule code and optional detail, then derive quarantine from those violations.
findings.prior_knowledge: Dictionaries/lists and DataFrame selection.

findings.title: A behavioral governance property is attributed to an unconstrained mutable container.
findings.evidence: The lesson defines audit trail as append-only—events are never modified or deleted—but the only implementation is a normal Python list, which permits assignment, deletion, insert and clear with no guard or persistence.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can believe that storing events in a list makes the record append-only or tamper-resistant.
findings.fix: State that the in-memory list models event order by convention only; expose only an append API in the lab and defer durable/tamper-evident enforcement, or implement a constrained append-only writer.
findings.prior_knowledge: Lists are mutable from S6.

findings.title: The learner must decode domain jargon while also learning the quality mechanism.
findings.evidence: Operational English terms such as `cap`, `runbook`, `stakeholder`, `schema drift` and `cross-field` appear with uneven Spanish explanation. Some core terms are defined, but these remain necessary to interpret the gate policy.
findings.impact: Due to this problem, a reasonable learner can understand the code yet not know what a `cap`, `runbook` or cross-field rule is supposed to mean operationally.
findings.fix: Introduce Spanish-first once: `tope (cap)`, `manual operativo (runbook)`, `parte interesada/responsable (stakeholder)`, `desviación de esquema (schema drift)`, `regla entre campos (cross-field)`.
findings.prior_knowledge: General Spanish and earlier Python/data vocabulary; these operations terms are not baseline knowledge.

findings.title: A learner can label value-versus-missing sources as consistent when the attribute contract expects agreement.
findings.evidence: SeriesGroupBy.nunique defaults dropna=True. For one key with ['Lima', None], the canonical expression returns count 1.
findings.impact: A learner can label value-versus-missing sources as consistent when the attribute contract expects agreement.
findings.fix: Declare missing semantics per attribute; preclassify null disagreement or use dropna=False when missing is a distinct state.

findings.title: A learner can let typos/new category codes enter clean data without an unmapped-category signal.
findings.evidence: cat_map.get(x.upper(), x.title()) promotes every unknown non-null token to a clean-looking title-cased category.
findings.impact: A learner can let typos/new category codes enter clean data without an unmapped-category signal.
findings.fix: Normalize text, then validate against the category map/allowlist; unknown values get an explicit reason.

findings.title: A learner can keep ordered events that still cannot reconstruct which run/input/rules they audit.
findings.evidence: Events contain event/n/reason but no run_id, timestamp, source/input hash, contract version or row/rule references.
findings.impact: A learner can keep ordered events that still cannot reconstruct which run/input/rules they audit.
findings.fix: Add run_id, observed_at, input/source id+hash, contract_version and row/rule references.

findings.title: No technical misconception, but accessibility-facing copy and editorial consistency remain below publication standard.
findings.evidence: Figure alt says 'politicas' without accent and learner copy alternates portfolio/portafolio.
findings.impact: No technical misconception, but accessibility-facing copy and editorial consistency remain below publication standard.
findings.fix: Use 'políticas' and standardize 'portafolio'.

findings.title: Learner can carry duplicated/quarantined rows or invalid canonical keys into joins and treat the aggregates as analysis-ready.
findings.evidence: S17 assumes a clean dataset and clean keys from S16, while effective S16 leaves clean/quarantine partitioning, money/category normalization, schema enforcement and provenance non-USABLE.
findings.impact: Learner can carry duplicated/quarantined rows or invalid canonical keys into joins and treat the aggregates as analysis-ready.
findings.fix: Add an S17 entry preflight proving disjoint clean/quarantine, non-null normalized join keys and required schema before merge.

findings.title: Missing cliente_id can match missing transaction ids and manufacture false relationships while validate passes.
findings.evidence: No null-key policy exists. pandas matches null merge keys to null keys. A one-null left key can be is_unique and pass one_to_many; is_unique and nunique()==len disagree because nunique drops missing by default.
findings.impact: Missing cliente_id can match missing transaction ids and manufacture false relationships while validate passes.
findings.fix: Reject/quarantine null join keys before merge; explain pandas null-match behavior and use one uniqueness check after missing policy.

findings.title: Learner can join on the wrong right-hand key/index and obtain plausible misalignment.
findings.evidence: `merge` and `join` are grouped as interchangeable key joins. DataFrame.join is index-oriented by default and join(on=key) matches the caller column to the other frame Index; S15 already left this unsafe.
findings.impact: Learner can join on the wrong right-hand key/index and obtain plausible misalignment.
findings.fix: Teach merge(on=...) as primary column-key operation; separately microdefine DataFrame.join index semantics with set_index.

findings.title: Learner can treat validate as an after-the-fact debugging stunt instead of a routine executable contract.
findings.evidence: The normal client-to-transactions 1:m merge omits validate; the only theory validate call deliberately fails one_to_one.
findings.impact: Learner can treat validate as an after-the-fact debugging stunt instead of a routine executable contract.
findings.fix: Use validate='one_to_many' on the canonical successful join, then contrast with a failing contract.

findings.title: Learner can inspect a left merge for right_only, see none and incorrectly conclude no orphan transactions exist.
findings.evidence: Text promises C002 left orphan and C003 right orphan, but code uses how='left'; that result cannot contain right_only and only prints C002.
findings.impact: Learner can inspect a left merge for right_only, see none and incorrectly conclude no orphan transactions exist.
findings.fix: Use outer+indicator or two explicit bilateral anti joins and print both sides with denominators.

findings.title: Learner can be surprised by inserted missing values, duplicate columns or index alignment that does not follow physical row position.
findings.evidence: Concat is an explicit outcome but has no theory worked example. One sentence omits alignment on the non-concatenation axis and default outer label behavior; S15 concat semantics were already unsafe.
findings.impact: Learner can be surprised by inserted missing values, duplicate columns or index alignment that does not follow physical row position.
findings.fix: Add axis=0 and axis=1 worked examples with mismatched labels, including join/ignore_index/keys.

findings.title: Learner can believe melt→pivot_table(sum) is an information-preserving inverse because the total still matches.
findings.evidence: Figure/prose frame wide and long as the same data and send melt output 'de regreso' through pivot_table. pivot_table aggregates duplicate index/column combinations and can destroy row-level detail; pivot instead requires uniqueness.
findings.impact: Learner can believe melt→pivot_table(sum) is an information-preserving inverse because the total still matches.
findings.fix: Teach pivot as reshape with unique pairs and pivot_table as reshape-plus-aggregation; add a duplicate-pair counterexample.

findings.title: Learner can publish segmented totals that silently omit unclassified rows and misread the residual as unexplained loss.
findings.evidence: No missing-group policy is declared. pandas GroupBy defaults dropna=True, so rows with missing region can contribute to raw totals yet disappear from regional parts without an exception.
findings.impact: Learner can publish segmented totals that silently omit unclassified rows and misread the residual as unexplained loss.
findings.fix: Explicitly quarantine, bucket or group missing keys with dropna=False and reconcile included/excluded rows.

findings.title: Learner can use transaction rows as a client denominator and produce misleading rates/averages.
findings.evidence: Prose discusses client counts, but code has no cliente_id and defines n=('monto','size'), which counts rows/transactions, not unique clients.
findings.impact: Learner can use transaction rows as a client denominator and produce misleading rates/averages.
findings.fix: Add cliente_id and publish n_rows=size separately from n_clientes=nunique.

findings.title: Learner can abandon the earlier exact-money contract during aggregation/reconciliation without understanding precision tradeoffs.
findings.evidence: Amounts are repeatedly labeled PEN but represented as Python floats and reconciled with float eps. S02 established Decimal for soles and S17 introduces no explicit analytical conversion boundary.
findings.impact: Learner can abandon the earlier exact-money contract during aggregation/reconciliation without understanding precision tradeoffs.
findings.fix: Keep canonical PEN as Decimal, or explicitly teach/preserve a Decimal→analytical-float boundary and its precision policy.

findings.title: Learner can hand-enter matching totals, get ok=True and believe a broken pipeline is reconciled.
findings.evidence: Code hand-authors total=100 and parts 60/30/10 in a fresh object; neither is derived from T1-T3. Therefore the claimed upstream fan-out cannot make this check fail.
findings.impact: Learner can hand-enter matching totals, get ok=True and believe a broken pipeline is reconciled.
findings.fix: Use one shared fixture: source total → validated join → aggregate → explicit exclusions/residual → reconstructed total.

findings.title: A prose approximation is formatted as executable Python inside the core fan-out gate, creating false syntax/semantics.
findings.evidence: The learner-facing contract writes `len(out) >> len(left)` in code formatting to mean 'much greater than'. In Python `>>` is the bitwise right-shift operator, not a comparison. Spot-check: `3 >> 2 == 0` and `10 >> 2 == 2`.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede copiar `len(out) >> len(left)` as a fan-out condition and get an integer bit-shift result—often zero—instead of a boolean comparison, or learn that `>>` means 'much greater than' in Python.
findings.fix: Do not put `>>` in code formatting. Write 'si `len(out)` es mucho mayor que `len(left)`' in prose, or better define an explicit expected row count/cardinality invariant and compare with `!=`, `>`, or a documented threshold.
findings.prior_knowledge: The learner knows ordinary comparison syntax from earlier sections; bitwise shifting is neither needed nor taught here.

findings.title: The prose, executable code and expected output describe different examples and different window sizes.
findings.evidence: The paragraph says the case contains transactions from January through March 2024 and uses a moving average with `window=2`. The code contains only 2024-01-01 through 2024-01-04 and executes `rolling(3)`. Its output `[nan, nan, 2.0, 3.0]` matches a three-observation window; a two-observation window on [1,2,3,4] would yield `[nan, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5]`.
findings.impact: Debido a este problema, un alumno razonable puede predict the output from the written `window=2` explanation, obtain a different canonical output, and conclude that rolling-window behavior is opaque or memorize the wrong window semantics.
findings.fix: Choose one example and keep all three surfaces identical: either change prose to January 1–4 with `window=3`, or change code/output to a two-observation or Jan–Mar example. Then explicitly say whether the window is observation-count or time-based.
findings.prior_knowledge: This subtopic is the first place S17 is responsible for making rolling-window semantics predictable.

findings.title: Learner can diagnose the wrong failure surface or assume a successful merge proves semantic alignment.
findings.evidence: Callout says str-int join produces false orphans; current pandas commonly rejects string/object versus integer merge keys with ValueError before an orphan table exists.
findings.impact: Learner can diagnose the wrong failure surface or assume a successful merge proves semantic alignment.
findings.fix: Say incompatible dtypes may raise; compatible text can still mismatch semantically. Normalize and validate representation plus values.
findings.attack: The callout categorically says a str↔int join produces false orphans.
findings.defense: The exact failure surface depends on pandas version and concrete dtypes: a mismatch may raise before merge or may yield non-matches when representations are comparable/object-like.

findings.title: Learner can try to detect duplicate-key fan-out with left_only/right_only instead of uniqueness/cardinality checks.
findings.evidence: Callout says 'anti-join de duplicados' although the lesson elsewhere correctly defines anti-join as unmatched rows and fan-out/duplicates as a different failure.
findings.impact: Learner can try to detect duplicate-key fan-out with left_only/right_only instead of uniqueness/cardinality checks.
findings.fix: Say 'exporta las claves duplicadas y, por separado, los anti-joins de filas sin pareja'.

findings.title: Duplicate client rows can make the formula encode a false grain assumption.
findings.evidence: `len(long)==n_clientes*n_meses` only holds if each wide row is one unique client and all selected value columns are months; general melt count is source rows × value_vars.
findings.impact: Duplicate client rows can make the formula encode a false grain assumption.
findings.fix: Use len(wide)*len(value_vars), then separately assert unique client grain when intended.

findings.title: Learner can pass the declared schema gate with duplicate columns and later select/export ambiguous data.
findings.evidence: set(df.columns)==set(expected) discards multiplicity. Duplicate column labels can pass membership even though names are ambiguous.
findings.impact: Learner can pass the declared schema gate with duplicate columns and later select/export ambiguous data.
findings.fix: Check columns.is_unique, then missing/extra sets, and order separately when required.

findings.title: Learner can unnecessarily mutate the index or conclude resample is unavailable with a normal datetime column.
findings.evidence: Text says resample requires DatetimeIndex. DataFrame.resample also supports a datetime-like column with on= or a datetime-like MultiIndex level with level=.
findings.impact: Learner can unnecessarily mutate the index or conclude resample is unavailable with a normal datetime column.
findings.fix: Say resample needs a datetime-like index/level, or a DataFrame datetime column supplied via on=.

findings.title: Learner can call rolling(7) a seven-day measure on irregular data or use current-inclusive rolling as if it used only prior history.
findings.evidence: Prose mixes 'periodos' and '7d' while code uses rolling(3), which means three observations. Default rolling includes the current observation; prior-only/as-of rolling is not contrasted.
findings.impact: Learner can call rolling(7) a seven-day measure on irregular data or use current-inclusive rolling as if it used only prior history.
findings.fix: Contrast observation windows vs time windows and descriptive current-inclusive vs shift/closed-left prior-only windows.

findings.title: Learner can reproduce the cutoff demo yet still calculate historical transform/rolling features from the full dataset and call the workflow…
findings.evidence: T4-B demonstrates cutoff only with a separate sum; it does not govern transform or rolling introduced immediately before, and default rolling is current-inclusive.
findings.impact: Learner can reproduce the cutoff demo yet still calculate historical transform/rolling features from the full dataset and call the workflow leakage-safe.
findings.fix: Filter/as-of before the earlier aggregation/feature and show prior-only rolling; distinguish post-cutoff data from actual use of future information.
findings.attack: T4-B applies cutoff only to a separate sum and calls sum_total - sum_pre a delta de leakage.
findings.defense: The arithmetic correctly separates all-period from pre-cutoff totals.

findings.title: ZERO_TECH learner can understand code but not know what 'portfolio ejecutivo + EDA' or a causal claim is supposed to mean.
findings.evidence: EDA, portfolio, stakeholder and claims appear before Spanish-first definitions; EDA's dedicated mental model is S18. The quick dictionary omits these deliverable-bearing terms.
findings.impact: ZERO_TECH learner can understand code but not know what 'portfolio ejecutivo + EDA' or a causal claim is supposed to mean.
findings.fix: First use: análisis exploratorio de datos (EDA), portafolio, parte interesada/destinatario (stakeholder), afirmación causal; keep S18 as deeper EDA.

findings.title: A learner can infer that a left-join row count tracks transaction rows and that unexpected growth indicates only bad data, not an incorrect…
findings.impact: A learner can infer that a left-join row count tracks transaction rows and that unexpected growth indicates only bad data, not an incorrect key/how/cardinality assumption.
findings.fix: Qualify the opening and use a discriminative fixture where len(cli), len(tx) and len(left_merge) are visibly different; print bilateral orphan counts separately.
findings.attack: The opening begins No es un error del código, while the first fixture prints cli=2, tx=3, merge=3. The left result equals tx length only by coincidence: one right orphan is excluded while one zero-match left client contributes a null row.
findings.defense: opening.p2 later explains that expected counts depend on join type and that right-side orphans do not enter a left join.

findings.title: A learner can classify an existing customer as newly acquired merely because the dataset starts after that customer's true first purchase, t…
findings.impact: A learner can classify an existing customer as newly acquired merely because the dataset starts after that customer's true first purchase, then interpret retention using the false cohort.
findings.fix: Call the default result cohorte observada. Only call it first purchase/acquisition when the source contract guarantees complete history back to the true first event, and state the observation-window start.
findings.attack: The lesson computes cohort as min(fecha) and then gives mes de primera compra as its practical meaning, later connecting it to retention.
findings.defense: The prose also says primera observación válida, which is correct for the rows visible in the dataset.

findings.title: La apertura crea una falsa dicotomía: presenta el crecimiento como una propiedad de los datos y no deja visible que una clave, how o contrato mal elegidos también son defectos de la lógica del análisis.
findings.impact: ¿Si el número de filas crece, debo asumir que el código está bien y que el problema siempre está en los datos?
findings.fix: Calificar la afirmación desde la primera oración y ligar el conteo al grano, la cardinalidad y el tipo de join declarados.

findings.title: El fixture imprime 2 filas cli, 3 filas tx y 3 filas merge. La igualdad tx=merge ocurre solo porque una tx huérfana excluida queda compensada por el cliente sin tx que el left join conserva.
findings.impact: ¿Un left join desde clientes termina normalmente con tantas filas como la tabla de transacciones?
findings.fix: Usar conteos discriminativos y hacer visible por separado la cobertura de ambos lados.

findings.title: min(fecha) identifica la primera fecha que existe en el histórico cargado; el texto la equipara con primera compra sin declarar desde cuándo la fuente tiene historia completa.
findings.impact: ¿Esta fecha es realmente la primera compra del cliente o solo la primera que aparece en mi dataset?
findings.fix: Separar cohorte observada de cohorte de adquisición y declarar la cobertura histórica requerida.

findings.title: El caso pasa de primera observación disponible a lectura de retención sin registrar el inicio de cobertura de la fuente.
findings.impact: ¿Puedo interpretar 2024-01 como adquisición real si mi archivo solo empieza en enero de 2024?
findings.fix: Declarar ventana de observación y limitar la etiqueta al evento que los datos realmente soportan.

findings.title: sum_total - sum_pre mide cantidad posterior al corte; no demuestra por sí sola que esa cantidad haya contaminado un cálculo histórico.
findings.impact: ¿Todo dato posterior al cutoff es leakage aunque nunca se use en la métrica as-of?
findings.fix: Nombrar primero la masa post-cutoff y reservar leakage para una operación que usa futuro indebidamente.

findings.title: El ejemplo etiqueta 115 como total con leakage sin mostrar primero la métrica histórica que se construyó incorrectamente usando febrero.
findings.impact: ¿Qué operación concreta filtró mal o incorporó futuro?
findings.fix: Mostrar explícitamente el cálculo incorrecto, el cálculo as-of correcto y transferir la frontera a una ventana/feature.

findings.title: Controls are taught as isolated checks instead of one end-to-end conservation chain over one shared fixture.
Important pandas defaults/semantics remain omitted or overgeneralized: null-key matching, missing-group exclusion, pivot_table aggregation, rolling boundaries and join/index behavior.
Business labels outrun the evidence: n means rows while prose says clients, observed minimum becomes first purchase, and post-cutoff mass becomes leakage.
A learner can perform careful statistics on a contaminated or incorrectly joined universe and mistake downstream precision for upstream vali…
findings.evidence: The lesson opens with 'El dataset ya está limpio y unido', but S17 remains REPAIR_REQUIRED: its clean inheritance, bilateral orphan evidence, missing-key policy and reconciliation are not safe.
findings.impact: A learner can perform careful statistics on a contaminated or incorrectly joined universe and mistake downstream precision for upstream validity.
findings.fix: Replace the inherited assertion with an entry preflight: verify S17 row universe, join coverage, exclusions and reconciliation evidence before EDA.

findings.title: A learner can think the true mean itself randomly moves inside the realized interval or that the realized interval assigns 95% probability t…
findings.evidence: The opening says a confidence interval tells 'en qué rango se mueve razonablemente el valor real'. Under the frequentist model taught later, the population parameter is fixed; repeated samples make the interval vary. T2-B later gives the more defensible parameter-under-sampling-model interpretation.
findings.impact: A learner can think the true mean itself randomly moves inside the realized interval or that the realized interval assigns 95% probability to the fixed parameter.
findings.fix: At first use, define the confidence level through repeated-sampling coverage and then translate to cautious language about parameter values compatible with the data/model.

findings.title: A learner can infer that exact-money rules disappear as soon as analysis starts, without knowing when conversion is acceptable or how reconc…
findings.evidence: S02 established Decimal for soles and S17 was already flagged for silently returning to float. S18 continues with float arrays and arithmetic on amounts in PEN without declaring a Decimal-to-analytical-float boundary or precision policy.
findings.impact: A learner can infer that exact-money rules disappear as soon as analysis starts, without knowing when conversion is acceptable or how reconciliation precision is protected.
findings.fix: State the analytical boundary explicitly: canonical money remains Decimal; if NumPy float copies are used for descriptive analysis, document conversion, non-ledger purpose and comparison/reconciliation policy.
findings.location: T1/T2/T3 code using NumPy/Pandas floats for PEN

findings.title: A learner can declare a sample unbiased after matching regional quotas, or quantify KPI bias using only share differences without any outcom…
findings.evidence: The lesson calls region share differences `bias_pp` and treats max absolute share difference as a risk measure for generalization. Marginal composition mismatch is a representativeness diagnostic, not the bias of a KPI estimator: matching region shares cannot rule out selection within regions, and differing shares need not bias an outcome if outcome distributions do not differ by region.
findings.impact: A learner can declare a sample unbiased after matching regional quotas, or quantify KPI bias using only share differences without any outcome relationship.
findings.fix: Rename to `share_diff_pp` or composition imbalance; explain that it diagnoses one observed dimension of coverage but does not estimate selection bias in the target metric.

findings.title: A learner can preregister repeated p<0.05 peeking and believe the preregistration alone makes the inference valid.
findings.evidence: The lesson correctly demonstrates that ten unadjusted interim looks inflate false positives, then says to fix metric, duration and stopping criterion before starting. Predeclaring an invalid 'stop at first p<0.05' rule does not restore a 5% type-I error; a valid sequential design/alpha-spending rule or a single fixed final look is required.
findings.impact: A learner can preregister repeated p<0.05 peeking and believe the preregistration alone makes the inference valid.
findings.fix: State the safe beginner rule as one fixed final analysis; if interim stopping is needed, require an explicitly sequentially valid procedure rather than ordinary repeated p-values.

findings.title: A learner can rank regions by tiny-sample anomaly rates and infer meaningful differences from one flagged observation.
findings.evidence: The paragraph says anomaly rates must report n by segment, while the code prints only {'Madrid': 0.2, 'Lima': 0.0}; each segment has n=5. This directly violates the section's promise that numbers carry n/coverage/uncertainty and invites comparison of 1/5 versus 0/5 as if stable.
findings.impact: A learner can rank regions by tiny-sample anomaly rates and infer meaningful differences from one flagged observation.
findings.fix: Print count, n and rate together per segment and attach an uncertainty/low-n warning or suppress comparative ranking below a declared minimum.

findings.title: A learner can cite a perfectly reproducible number as evidence for the wrong business question—the exact traceability failure T4-A claims to…
findings.evidence: The paragraph asks about Lima. The code prints the question 'Madrid', while `metrica` is `median(monto | region==Lima)`. The output therefore contains a question and calculation referring to different populations.
findings.impact: A learner can cite a perfectly reproducible number as evidence for the wrong business question—the exact traceability failure T4-A claims to prevent.
findings.fix: Use one region consistently in question, filter, result and output and add an assertion tying the declared segment to the actual filter.

findings.title: A learner can satisfy the traceability template by typing plausible evidence into a dict rather than deriving it from data, while claiming a…
findings.evidence: The example contains no dataset or statistic calculation. `n=40`, `median=27.5` and `(24,31)` are hand-authored, while the prose claims a documented bootstrap interval. The field name `ic95_z_or_boot` further refuses to say which method generated it.
findings.impact: A learner can satisfy the traceability template by typing plausible evidence into a dict rather than deriving it from data, while claiming a bootstrap that never ran.
findings.fix: Build the T4-A result from a shared fixture, execute a median bootstrap, store `method='bootstrap_percentile'`, B, seed, n and calculated endpoints, then print the trace.

findings.title: A learner can document a filter that was never executed and later use the note as false provenance evidence.
findings.evidence: The note records `filtros: ['monto > 0']`, but the code never applies that filter. It hashes and summarizes the unfiltered DataFrame. The current all-positive fixture hides the lie because applying the filter would happen to keep all rows.
findings.impact: A learner can document a filter that was never executed and later use the note as false provenance evidence.
findings.fix: Execute the declared filter from code, record n_pre/n_post and hash the exact analysis payload after the transformation (plus source hash separately if needed).

findings.title: A learner can pass the final lesson example while failing most of the reproducibility requirements stated immediately above it.
findings.evidence: The paragraph contract requires pandas/numpy versions, relative paths, outputs, seed, schema, n pre/post, payload hash and generalization limits. The note code stores only origin, cutoff, one n, filter text, unused seed and a hash; it omits versions, schema, pre/post counts, actual cutoff enforcement and limits.
findings.impact: A learner can pass the final lesson example while failing most of the reproducibility requirements stated immediately above it.
findings.fix: Make the code instantiate every required field from executed operations; the final theory example must be the executable version of the contract, not a partial sketch.

findings.title: A learner can use mean-minus-median as a tail detector without inspecting the distribution and can overstate median invariance.
findings.evidence: The paragraph states that a large mean-median separation is itself a finding that 'la distribución tiene cola' and says the median 'no se inmuta' before one extreme. Separation can suggest skew/outliers/mixtures but does not uniquely diagnose a tail, and a changed observation can affect the median if it crosses ranks near the center.
findings.impact: A learner can use mean-minus-median as a tail detector without inspecting the distribution and can overstate median invariance.
findings.fix: Say the separation is a signal to inspect skewness, outliers or mixtures; describe median as resistant, not immovable.

findings.title: A learner can compare p90 values across tools or reports and treat method-driven differences as data changes.
findings.evidence: The n=7 fixture reports p90=75 as though p90 were uniquely defined. NumPy supports multiple quantile estimation methods and defaults to method='linear'; methods can differ materially in small samples.
findings.impact: A learner can compare p90 values across tools or reports and treat method-driven differences as data changes.
findings.fix: For small samples, name the quantile convention (`method='linear'`) and note that tail quantiles are unstable/interpolation-sensitive at n=7.

findings.title: A learner can transform refunds/negative corrections into NaN or silently filter them only to make the transform work.
findings.evidence: The lesson recommends `log1p` for monetary amounts without declaring the admissible domain or what happens to zero/negative adjustments. NumPy computes log(1+x) and returns NaN for real inputs outside the real-valued domain; later text explicitly lists `monto>0` as a possible filter, proving sign policy is relevant.
findings.impact: A learner can transform refunds/negative corrections into NaN or silently filter them only to make the transform work.
findings.fix: Declare the business/sign policy before log transform; preserve excluded/refund rows as a separate population and never let the mathematical domain choose the business universe silently.

findings.title: A learner can report unit-inconsistent differences and confuse proportions, percentage points and percent change.
findings.evidence: `0.80 - 0.55 = 0.25` is printed/labeled as `bias_pp`. If `pp` means percentage points, the value is +25 pp, not +0.25 pp; +0.25 is a proportion difference.
findings.impact: A learner can report unit-inconsistent differences and confuse proportions, percentage points and percent change.
findings.fix: Either output `share_diff=0.25` or multiply by 100 and output `share_diff_pp=25.0`.

findings.title: A learner can memorize 1.96 with sample standard deviation as the universal 95% mean interval and apply it to smaller samples where the dist…
findings.evidence: The basic mean interval is taught as mean ± 1.96·s/√n. With unknown population standard deviation and sample s, the standard finite-sample interval uses a t critical value; z is an approximation as n grows. The code labels itself z_approx, but the prose makes it the primary formula.
findings.impact: A learner can memorize 1.96 with sample standard deviation as the universal 95% mean interval and apply it to smaller samples where the distinction matters.
findings.fix: Teach t·s/√n as the baseline when sigma is unknown; present z=1.96 explicitly as a large-n approximation or known-sigma case.

findings.title: A learner can treat a low-replication bootstrap endpoint as precise and mistake simulation noise for inferential information.
findings.evidence: The lesson prints a percentile 95% bootstrap interval from only 200 replicates as a stable expected output. Authoritative introductory guidance commonly uses at least hundreds more (e.g. 500-1000) because tail percentiles themselves have Monte Carlo variability.
findings.impact: A learner can treat a low-replication bootstrap endpoint as precise and mistake simulation noise for inferential information.
findings.fix: Use at least 1000-2000 replicates for the teaching output and mention Monte Carlo error; keep the seed for reproducibility.

findings.title: A learner can reuse the formula on unequal groups and report the wrong standardized effect size.
findings.evidence: The code names `sp` as pooled standard deviation but computes sqrt((sa²+sb²)/2), which equals the usual sample-size-weighted pooled SD only when the two group sizes are equal. The fixture hides this by using 40/40.
findings.impact: A learner can reuse the formula on unequal groups and report the wrong standardized effect size.
findings.fix: Either state that the shown shortcut is equal-n only or implement the weighted pooled-variance formula using n_a and n_b.

findings.title: A learner can treat a narrow interval as a decision gate even when the sample is biased, the effect is practically irrelevant or the action…
findings.evidence: The figure says two studies have the same headline and 'Solo uno de ellos permite actuar' because one interval is narrower. T4-A correctly says a business decision also requires cost, risk and coverage. Precision alone does not authorize action.
findings.impact: A learner can treat a narrow interval as a decision gate even when the sample is biased, the effect is practically irrelevant or the action has unmodeled costs/risks.
findings.fix: Caption it as 'solo uno estima con suficiente precisión para considerar la siguiente decisión, sujeto a cobertura, magnitud, costo y riesgo'.

findings.title: A learner can think an 'instrument' is any extra variable/control or seek an advanced causal method without its assumptions.
findings.evidence: The prose says to list designs that would break causes, '(experimento, instrumento)', but 'instrumento' is not introduced or explained and instrumental-variable identification is materially more advanced than the surrounding EDA contract.
findings.impact: A learner can think an 'instrument' is any extra variable/control or seek an advanced causal method without its assumptions.
findings.fix: Remove the term here or add only a bounded forward reference: instrumental variables are a later causal design requiring specific relevance/exclusion assumptions.

findings.title: A learner can cargo-cult the manual rank code onto real data with ties and calculate a non-Spearman coefficient.
findings.evidence: The demo implements ranks with `np.argsort(np.argsort(x))`, which assigns distinct ordinal positions to tied values. Standard Spearman ranking handles ties by assigning shared/average ranks. The unique-valued fixture prevents the defect from appearing.
findings.impact: A learner can cargo-cult the manual rank code onto real data with ties and calculate a non-Spearman coefficient.
findings.fix: Use a tie-safe rank implementation (`scipy.stats.rankdata`/`spearmanr`) or explicitly state the toy implementation assumes no ties and add a tied counterexample.

findings.title: A learner can interpret a higher segment rate as more internally anomalous when it may simply have a different legitimate level/scale.
findings.evidence: Tukey fences are computed globally and then anomaly rates are compared by region. A global rule can be legitimate, but if segment baselines differ it measures distance from the pooled distribution, not unusualness within each segment. The lesson never states which question is intended.
findings.impact: A learner can interpret a higher segment rate as more internally anomalous when it may simply have a different legitimate level/scale.
findings.fix: Declare whether thresholds are global business rules or within-segment descriptive fences; do not compare the resulting rates as though those meanings were interchangeable.

findings.title: A learner can put a positional index in an evidence memo and be unable to locate the same record after a harmless transformation.
findings.evidence: The prose promises an anomaly 'en ese id' and the portfolio lists `ids_anom`, but the DataFrame has no entity/ticket id. The code outputs the transient row index `[7]`, which changes after filtering, sorting or reindexing.
findings.impact: A learner can put a positional index in an evidence memo and be unable to locate the same record after a harmless transformation.
findings.fix: Add a stable synthetic `ticket_id` and emit that key; never call a transient DataFrame index an id unless index identity is itself a declared contract.

findings.title: A learner can think each row is fingerprinted or treat a short display token as strong provenance identity.
findings.evidence: `row_sha1_8` is not a row hash; it is the first eight hex characters of SHA-1 over the entire CSV serialization. Eight hex characters provide only 32 bits of fingerprint space and the serialization itself can vary with formatting/version choices.
findings.impact: A learner can think each row is fingerprinted or treat a short display token as strong provenance identity.
findings.fix: Rename to `analysis_payload_sha256`, use a canonical serialization plus full SHA-256 (optionally display a longer prefix), and separately define row hashes only if row-level identity is required.

findings.title: A learner can execute the syntax while being unable to explain why n-1 appears, what population is reachable by the frame, what pooled SD me…
findings.evidence: Terms carrying operational meaning appear without sufficient local introduction, notably `ddof`, sampling `marco`, `s_pooled`, causal `instrumento`, and provenance `hash`. Several are not mere API spelling: they determine denominator, inference or evidence semantics.
findings.impact: A learner can execute the syntax while being unable to explain why n-1 appears, what population is reachable by the frame, what pooled SD means, what an instrument is, or what exactly the hash attests to.
findings.fix: Add Spanish-first microdefinitions at first meaningful use and remove advanced terms whose assumptions are not taught in S18.

findings.title: S19 opens by treating S18 outputs as already trustworthy
findings.evidence: Opening: 'El EDA de S18 dejó medianas, tamaños de muestra e incertidumbre.'
findings.impact: Learner can chart S18 artifacts whose denominators, intervals, provenance and traceability are still unresolved, laundering upstream uncertainty into polished figures.
findings.fix: Make the handoff conditional: first verify S18 data note, denominator, uncertainty method and exact analytical payload before visualization.

findings.title: The claimed visual-inflation factor is never calculated
findings.evidence: T1-B says calculate '(altura_truco / altura_honesta)'; code prints 0.67 and 0.10 separately. Their ratio, the actual inflation factor under that definition, is 6.67.
findings.impact: A central integrity gate appears executable but does not produce the metric named by the prose.
findings.fix: Define the metric precisely and print `factor_inflacion = ratio_truco / ratio_honesto` (=6.67 for the fixture), while explaining what the ratio represents and its limits.

findings.title: Matplotlib outcome promises bar-count verification but the canonical theory example omits it
findings.evidence: Outcome and T2-A prose name 'n de barras' / 'conteo de barras'; `mpl_bar.py` records axes/ylabel/ylim only.
findings.impact: The learner sees a stated executable contract that the worked example does not actually demonstrate.
findings.fix: Capture the returned BarContainer or inspect `ax.patches` and assert/print the expected number of bars.

findings.title: Export contract says savefig is required while the code only simulates metadata
findings.evidence: T2-B: 'Exporta de verdad con fig.savefig'; code comment says '# simular export metadata' and never calls savefig.
findings.impact: The exact skill named in the learning outcome—producing a versioned PNG—is not demonstrated, and a metadata dict can pass while no artifact exists.
findings.fix: Write to BytesIO or a temporary/versioned file with `fig.savefig(..., dpi=120, bbox_inches='tight')`; validate non-zero bytes/format and derive metadata from the created artifact.

findings.title: Interactive accessibility contract omits keyboard/focus and tooltip behavior
findings.evidence: T3-A minimal spec is `{filtro, tooltip_template, unidad, campos_visibles}` and discusses hover/tooltips but not keyboard focus, focus order, dismissibility, hoverability or persistence.
findings.impact: A dashboard can satisfy the lesson's spec while remaining unusable to keyboard and screen-reader users; this conflicts with the section's central accessibility claim.
findings.fix: Extend the spec with keyboard-reachable controls, focus-visible behavior, accessible names/state, tooltip trigger by focus as well as pointer, and WCAG 1.4.13 behavior when custom hover/focus content is used.

findings.title: Filter-driven conclusion recalculation and JSON state serialization are promised but not demonstrated
findings.evidence: T3-A contract requires recalculating conclusion and serializing state; `interactive_spec.py` only filters one row and prints a tooltip dict.
findings.impact: The example does not test the product defect the paragraph warns about, so a stale global conclusion would still pass.
findings.fix: Build a serializable state object, derive the filtered summary/conclusion from `vista`, serialize it with JSON, and test a second filter where the leader/conclusion changes.

findings.title: Active filter says Lima while accessible table and chart value describe Madrid
findings.evidence: T3-B code: `state['filtro_region']='Lima'`, while `alt_table[0]['region']='Madrid'` and `chart_value=28.0` matches the Madrid row.
findings.impact: The canonical accessibility example violates its own filtered-state parity contract.
findings.fix: Generate chart value, table row, alt text and sample metadata from the same filtered payload/state.

findings.title: The parity check is a one-scalar false positive
findings.evidence: `match = chart_value == alt_table[0]['ticket_mediano_pen']` prints True despite the Lima/Madrid state contradiction.
findings.impact: Learner is explicitly shown a green integrity gate that misses row identity, active filter, categories, n and precision—the failure modes the section claims to prevent.
findings.fix: Compare normalized chart-data and table-data records including key/category, metric, value, n, filter state and display precision; fail on missing/extra rows.

findings.title: Final alt text and the supposedly acceptable claim disagree about which region leads
findings.evidence: `alt` says Lima 28, Madrid 24, Bogota 22.5; `claim_ok` says Madrid has the highest median.
findings.impact: The section closes its no-overclaim lesson with a claim contradicted by its own evidence.
findings.fix: Derive the claim from the same rows used to build the alt/table; with the shown values the permitted claim must say Lima leads the sample.

findings.title: The nominal Peru case mixes Lima with Madrid, Bogota and Berlin as if they were peer Peruvian regions
findings.evidence: Job relevance warns against 'Madrid lidera el Perú'; examples repeatedly label a Peru case while using Madrid/Bogota/Berlin alongside Lima.
findings.impact: Breaks the localized mental model and makes population/generalization statements geographically incoherent.
findings.fix: Either use Peruvian peer geographies consistently (e.g. Lima/Arequipa/Trujillo) or explicitly define a multinational market dimension and stop saying 'del Perú'.

findings.title: T4-B contains an unscaffolded SQL/ML-leakage mini-lesson outside S19's roadmap
findings.evidence: After three accessibility/claims paragraphs, four additional paragraphs introduce Codd/SEQUEL, SQL fundamentals, sqlite3 and ML leakage. S19 roadmap assigns T4-B to color/contrast/alt/no-overclaim; SQL was already S12 and leakage has a later dedicated progression.
findings.impact: Adds cognitive load at the exact closure point, weakens narrative coherence and displaces practice on the section's actual accessibility gate.
findings.fix: Remove this detour from S19 theory or reduce it to a one-sentence provenance bridge; keep SQL teaching in its owning section and leakage in its dedicated ML progression.

findings.title: The leakage paragraph falsely says the learner saw ML Pipeline behavior in S09
findings.evidence: T4-B: 'En ML (como viste en S09)...'; current S09 canonical title is 'Excepciones, debugging y logging seguro'.
findings.impact: Creates a nonexistent prerequisite and leaves a zero-tech learner without the background the paragraph assumes.
findings.fix: Delete the S09 reference; if the material remains, introduce it self-sufficiently or point only to the actual later ML/leakage owner.

findings.title: 'Describe con todo' is unsafe guidance for a held-out test set
findings.evidence: T4-B rule: 'describe con todo, decide solo con lo que verías en producción.'
findings.impact: Inspecting a held-out test set during exploratory analysis can influence feature/model/threshold decisions and leak test information even without fit_transform.
findings.fix: Keep the final test set sealed from model-development EDA; explore train/development data, make decisions there, then use the test set only for the predeclared final evaluation.

findings.title: Audience guidance is framed as role stereotype rather than task and decision need
findings.evidence: Opening: 'Una gerencia necesita una idea y pocas categorías; un equipo de análisis aguanta más detalle.'
findings.impact: Teaches learners to simplify by job title instead of matching density to decision, time, expertise and consequence.
findings.fix: Define audience by decision, time budget, prior knowledge and required drill-down; role can be an example, not the rule.

findings.title: Encoding hierarchy is materially oversimplified
findings.evidence: T1-B: 'Jerarquía de encodings: posición > longitud > color > forma.'
findings.impact: Conflates quantitative accuracy with categorical channels and omits angle/area distinctions; learner may treat hue or shape as ordered quantitative encodings.
findings.fix: Teach position on common scale and length as strong quantitative channels; distinguish angle/area and explain that hue/shape are primarily categorical, not a universal numeric ranking.

findings.title: The multi-panel example silently applies the bar zero-baseline rule to a line chart
findings.evidence: T2-B loops over both axes and runs `ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)`, including the panel titled 'Tendencia'.
findings.impact: Learner may generalize 'all Y axes start at zero', although the section correctly scopes the strict zero rule to bar-length magnitude encodings.
findings.fix: Apply zero baseline to the bar panel only; teach line-axis choice from analytical purpose and provide sufficient contextual scale.

findings.title: Migration from a data spec to Plotly/Streamlit is called 'mechanical'
findings.evidence: T3-A and callout: 'si el modelo es claro, migrar a una librería interactiva es mecánico.'
findings.impact: Hides real work in event/state semantics, accessibility, keyboard behavior, responsiveness and library-specific rendering.
findings.fix: Say the spec reduces migration ambiguity but implementation still requires library-specific interaction and accessibility validation.

findings.title: Viewport sampling n and metric n are presented without distinct definitions
findings.evidence: T3-B state contains sample_n=5000/universe_n=50000 while the accessible row independently says n=40.
findings.impact: Learner cannot tell whether n means rendered points, analytical observations behind a statistic, or population coverage.
findings.fix: Name each denominator explicitly, e.g. `rendered_points_n`, `eligible_universe_n`, `metric_observations_n`, and state their relationship.

findings.title: The 'accessible table' contract stops at numeric parity and omits table semantics
findings.evidence: T3-B defines 'alternativa accesible = tabla ordenable + resumen textual' but never states headers/caption/row-column associations or keyboard-operable sorting.
findings.impact: A visually tabular or mouse-only sortable component could satisfy the prose yet remain inaccessible to assistive technology.
findings.fix: Add programmatic headers/caption and keyboard-operable sort-state requirements to the contract; numeric parity is necessary but not sufficient.

findings.title: Caption provenance is manually authored rather than bound to the analytical payload
findings.evidence: T4-A hardcodes source, cutoff, n and limitation in a dict; no dataset/data-note identifier, hash or derivation is checked.
findings.impact: A polished caption can drift away from the data it describes, especially because S18's data-note example is itself unresolved.
findings.fix: Build caption metadata from the validated S18 note/payload identity and carry a stable data-note or payload identifier into the figure manifest.

findings.title: 'Contraste suficiente' is not operationalized
findings.evidence: T4-B says 'Contraste suficiente texto/fondo' but gives no measurable threshold and does not distinguish text from graphical-object contrast.
findings.impact: Learner cannot test the requirement; subjective 'se ve bien' can pass despite WCAG failures.
findings.fix: Teach the relevant WCAG targets for normal/large text and required non-text graphical information, while preserving the non-color channel rule.

findings.title: SQL detour presents an overly categorical 'four fundamental operations' model
findings.evidence: T4-B: 'Las cuatro operaciones fundamentales de SQL son SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY y JOIN.'
findings.impact: Conflates clauses/operations and presents a narrow dashboard-query subset as the fundamentals of SQL.
findings.fix: If retained, call them four common clauses/operations for analytical SELECT queries, not the four fundamentals of SQL.

findings.title: SQL example defaults to AVG(ticket) without reconnecting to S18's robust-metric decision
findings.evidence: The detour's example uses `AVG(ticket)` immediately after S18 taught that skewed ticket values can make mean a poor 'typical' metric.
findings.impact: Learner can infer that the SQL layer licenses a different metric simply because AVG is convenient.
findings.fix: Tie the aggregation to the stated business question; if mean is used, say why. Otherwise show that robust metrics may require a different query/processing path.

findings.title: Spanish-first redaction is weakened by a dense cluster of unexplained or inconsistently translated terms
findings.evidence: Examples include chart, brief, encoding, dual-axis, faceting, state, sample, aggregate, claim, loop, gate, metadata and portfolio; T4-B also contains 'cambiaria' without the required accent 'cambiaría'.
findings.impact: Raises unnecessary lexical load for a zero-tech learner and breaks the course's self-sufficient Peruvian-Spanish contract.
findings.fix: Introduce Spanish first with the English term only where useful, reuse one stable translation, and correct grammar/accents.

findings.title: Learner is taught to trust lineage labels rather than verify artifact identity and denominator semantics.
findings.evidence: S20 says its row counts reconcile with S19 and its data note is aligned to S18, even though the running ledger marks S18 and S19 REPAIR_REQUIRED for denominator, parity and provenance defects.
findings.impact: Learner is taught to trust lineage labels rather than verify artifact identity and denominator semantics.
findings.fix: Require payload/data-note identity checks before consumption and state explicitly which S18/S19 fields must be revalidated.
findings.attack: S20 can turn unresolved upstream evidence into a polished workbook and thereby launder uncertainty into an apparently audited deliverable.
findings.defense: Cross-section continuity is intended, and later sections should reuse prior artifacts rather than rebuild everything.

findings.title: Learner exits S20 without two promised workbook-addressing constructs and may wrongly believe they are interchangeable with headers.
findings.evidence: Roadmap T1 explicitly owns 'tablas y named ranges'; the lesson says fixed headers + sheetnames are the practical equivalent and never teaches openpyxl Table or defined-name behavior.
findings.impact: Learner exits S20 without two promised workbook-addressing constructs and may wrongly believe they are interchangeable with headers.
findings.fix: Add a minimal real Table and defined-name example, including uniqueness/range validation and when each is preferable.
findings.attack: A binding learning target is explicitly replaced rather than taught.
findings.defense: Fixed headers and stable sheet names are simpler and sufficient for a minimal reporting factory.

findings.title: The learner cannot satisfy S20's own roadmap contract or distinguish worksheet/workbook protection from file security.
findings.evidence: Roadmap T2 requires styles, charts, templates, dates, merged cells and protection. S20 declares embedded Excel charts optional and contains no workbook/worksheet protection lesson or outcome.
findings.impact: The learner cannot satisfy S20's own roadmap contract or distinguish worksheet/workbook protection from file security.
findings.fix: Teach one minimal embedded chart path and one protection example, explicitly warning that worksheet/workbook protection prevents accidental editing but is not encryption.
findings.attack: Two roadmap-owned capabilities disappear from the authored theory.
findings.defense: S19 already creates PNG charts, and protection might be unnecessary for synthetic workbooks.

findings.title: The course labels the artifact robust without testing the human-visible deliverable.
findings.evidence: Roadmap T4 requires visual and structural tests. S20 teaches structural checks but no visual/render/open-in-Excel verification path.
findings.impact: The course labels the artifact robust without testing the human-visible deliverable.
findings.fix: Add a visual QA contract: render/screenshot through an available office engine or at minimum open/reload plus human review checklist with evidence path; keep structural tests separate.
findings.attack: A workbook can be structurally valid while visually broken, especially after template edits, merged cells, styles or unsupported object loss.
findings.defense: Headless CI cannot conveniently run Excel GUI, so structural tests are easier and more portable.

findings.title: Learner can preserve the master while silently damaging the generated copy, then report success because only the master hash was checked.
findings.evidence: The lesson treats copy→load_workbook→save as sufficient to keep the VP template intact. Current openpyxl documentation warns that it does not read all Excel objects and that shapes can be lost when existing files are opened and saved.
findings.impact: Learner can preserve the master while silently damaging the generated copy, then report success because only the master hash was checked.
findings.fix: Define a supported-template feature contract, reject unsupported objects, reopen and inventory the output, and visual-check the generated copy. Clarify that master immutability is not output fidelity.
findings.attack: The central gate 'sin dañar la plantilla' is not guaranteed by the chosen library workflow for arbitrary complex templates.
findings.defense: The synthetic course template is simple and the master bytes are hashed before/after, so the original file remains untouched.

findings.title: Structural checks can disagree while each claims to implement the same contract.
findings.evidence: Opening/reference declare Entrada, Datos, Salida canonical; T1 callout says Entrada + Salida is the minimum and Datos is optional; code and final manifest contain only Entrada/Salida.
findings.impact: Structural checks can disagree while each claims to implement the same contract.
findings.fix: Choose one schema: either make Datos required everywhere or define required versus optional sheets explicitly in one machine-readable contract.
findings.attack: There is no single workbook schema for the learner to validate.
findings.defense: Datos may reasonably be optional staging depending on the report.

findings.title: Learner can confuse a boolean label with evidence that rerun behavior was tested.
findings.evidence: The lesson says idempotence is checked by running twice and comparing. No theory example executes the factory twice; the final manifest simply sets 'idempotent': true.
findings.impact: Learner can confuse a boolean label with evidence that rerun behavior was tested.
findings.fix: Run the same fixture twice into clean/versioned outputs, compare canonical data/state fingerprints, assert no duplicate rows/styles, then derive the manifest field from that check.
findings.attack: The strongest operational property in the section is asserted rather than measured.
findings.defense: The final code is a manifest-schema illustration, not necessarily the complete factory implementation.

findings.title: Teaches decorative observability instead of evidence-derived observability.
findings.evidence: Prose says reconcile/structural/batch outcomes live in the manifest; the final manifest hardcodes reconcile_ok=true, backup path, sheets and idempotent=true without consuming the prior checks.
findings.impact: Teaches decorative observability instead of evidence-derived observability.
findings.fix: Build one run-result object from executed checks and serialize that exact object; never type success booleans manually.
findings.attack: The audit artifact can claim success even when the actual workbook failed.
findings.defense: The snippet may be intended only to demonstrate JSON shape.

findings.title: The claimed audit trail is not actually traceable end-to-end.
findings.evidence: Manifest identifies only a short input digest and string backup path. It lacks output workbook hash, template hash/version, script/git version, dependency versions and upstream S18/S19 payload identity.
findings.impact: The claimed audit trail is not actually traceable end-to-end.
findings.fix: Record full input/output/template SHA-256, git/script version, dependency versions, run id, upstream payload/data-note id and observed checks.
findings.attack: A reviewer cannot prove which template/code/payload produced a particular workbook or whether the manifest belongs to that output.
findings.defense: For a small synthetic lab, a compact manifest may be enough to teach the concept.

findings.title: Learner cannot predict what is actually serialized in the XLSX and may confuse Python display with workbook storage format.
findings.evidence: Text says dates are serialized ISO YYYY-MM-DD. Code assigns a Python date to a default Workbook. Audit execution with openpyxl 3.1.5 stored the cell as numeric Excel serial 45473; ISO storage required wb.iso_dates=True.
findings.impact: Learner cannot predict what is actually serialized in the XLSX and may confuse Python display with workbook storage format.
findings.fix: Either set wb.iso_dates=True and verify the saved/reopened file, or change the prose to say date/datetime values are written with an explicitly documented Excel date representation.
findings.attack: The code demonstrates a different file representation than the stated contract.
findings.defense: When reloaded through openpyxl, the value becomes a Python date and prints isoformat(), so user-visible semantics remain date-like.

findings.title: Cross-section semantic drift leaves the learner unable to know which numeric rule is authoritative for money.
findings.evidence: S20 reconciles PEN with float and abs(diff)<0.01. S02 explicitly states not to use float for soles and teaches Decimal constructed from strings.
findings.impact: Cross-section semantic drift leaves the learner unable to know which numeric rule is authoritative for money.
findings.fix: Use Decimal/integer cents for the reconciliation boundary, or explicitly teach and test a controlled Decimal↔analytical numeric conversion policy before using float.
findings.attack: A later reporting/finance lesson silently reverses an earlier money-representation contract at the exact point where cent-level reconciliation matters.
findings.defense: Pandas often uses float analytics and a cent tolerance can be pragmatic for reporting data.

findings.title: Learner can pass the gate without validating the generated workbook.
findings.evidence: Contract requires sum_xlsx versus sum_df and n_xlsx==n_df, with reconcile_ok in manifest. Code compares a DataFrame total to hardcoded tot_portada=22.0, never reads an XLSX output, never checks n, and only prints ok.
findings.impact: Learner can pass the gate without validating the generated workbook.
findings.fix: Generate/reopen the output workbook, read the exact total and data-row count from it, compare both to the validated source payload, and derive reconcile_ok.
findings.attack: The executable example does not test the artifact it claims to reconcile.
findings.defense: The hardcoded portada value is a minimal stand-in for a workbook cell.

findings.title: Reintroduces an unresolved S17 missing-group defect into the executive reporting layer.
findings.evidence: The materialized pivot uses pandas groupby('region') with default dropna=True. Audit probe with one missing region retained source total 22.0 but visible grouped total fell to 17.0; dropna=False restored 22.0.
findings.impact: Reintroduces an unresolved S17 missing-group defect into the executive reporting layer.
findings.fix: Validate region non-null as a precondition or use dropna=False and surface the missing-key group; reconcile the pivot total itself to source.
findings.attack: A reporting pivot can silently omit money while a separate source-total reconciliation still passes.
findings.defense: Earlier quality gates may forbid missing regions before S20.

findings.title: Creates a false-green structural gate and teaches misleading test naming.
findings.evidence: Prose requires required-sheet subset, exact headers, domain rules and manifest status. Code names its print structure_ok but only evaluates headers==expected and one synthetic allowlist row; it does not inspect sheetnames or serialize failure evidence.
findings.impact: Creates a false-green structural gate and teaches misleading test naming.
findings.fix: Implement separate sheets_ok, headers_ok, domains_ok, aggregate structural_ok=all(...), and store violators plus the policy decision in the manifest.
findings.attack: The label 'structure_ok' is broader than the predicate actually tested.
findings.defense: Each sub-check could be composed later in the complete project.

findings.title: Learner may believe PermissionError-on-open is the universal Excel-lock contract.
findings.evidence: The batch example classifies locks only because fake_open raises PermissionError when a filename contains 'lock'. Real Excel/shared-file lock behavior varies by platform and operation; Microsoft documents files can be locked for editing while still openable/readable.
findings.impact: Learner may believe PermissionError-on-open is the universal Excel-lock contract.
findings.fix: Teach lock handling as an adapter boundary: detect known owner/temp files where relevant, catch write/open permission failures, record operation+exception, and test the policy through injected filesystem behaviors without claiming one universal lock mechanism.
findings.attack: The demo proves a fake exception branch, not robust handling of an actual locked workbook or save conflict.
findings.defense: A deterministic fake is appropriate for a portable unit-level lesson and avoids OS-specific flakiness.

findings.title: The student learns one corruption symptom as if it were the corruption category.
